author: Kewei
subject: cl, execution: fix two causes of a stall after a Caplin restart (#24628)
body:
## Summary

Two fixes for one restart failure of an Erigon node with embedded
Caplin, one commit each. Both showed up in the same devnet scenario:
with only the second fix, the first problem caused a longer stall.

1. **Block collector finality (cl).** After each batch and at the end of
`Flush`, when the last inserted block was above the EL's head, Caplin's
block collector sent the EL a fork-choice update with that block as
head, safe and finalized. The collector does not know the consensus
checkpoints, and that block is not necessarily finalized. The EL stores
the finalized hash, refuses any reorg below it, and can prune changesets
below it. The collector now sends zero safe and finalized hashes. The EL
does not overwrite its stored markers with zero hashes, so they keep
their previous values until a fork-choice update that moves the head
stores the real checkpoints.
2. **Revalidating an executed canonical block (execution).**
`ValidateChain` unwound to the requested block before
`ForkValidator.ValidatePayload` returned VALID for it as a canonical
block, so the unwind did no useful work. Once the changesets needed for
that unwind had been pruned, `UnwindTo` refused it with `too far unwind`
and `ValidateChain` returned that error. After a restart, Caplin's Gloas
verification sweep calls NewPayload again for payloads it has not
recorded as verified, which can include old canonical ones. After the
existing missing-data and `MaxReorgDepth` checks, `ValidateChain` now
returns VALID, with the block as latest valid hash, when the block is
canonical at its number, at or below the fork-choice finalized block,
and executed (Execution stage progress >= its number). Above the
finalized block the canonical marker is not enough: the state-ahead
recovery in `updateForkChoice` can mark a fork canonical without
executing it. Side-fork blocks, canonical blocks above the finalized
block, and blocks not yet executed take the existing path. On
NewPayload, the direct execution client returns NotValidated for blocks
more than `reorgTooDeepDepth` (3) below the head before it calls
`ValidateChain`, and the engine server's quick path already answers
VALID for a stored canonical block, so the new fast path fires only when
the stored finalized marker is within 3 blocks of the head: in practice,
a datadir that still holds a false marker from an older build, or a
Gloas stretch where nearly every slot's payload is EMPTY.

The collector commit comes first: the second fix trusts canonical blocks
at or below the stored finalized block, and the first stops the
collector from storing a false one.

Devnet: Kurtosis, Fulu at genesis, Gloas at epoch 2 (slot 64), 12 s
slots; Lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0, Teku 26.9.1, Prysm v7.2.0, Nimbus
v26.10.0 and two Erigon/Caplin nodes. The Erigon node with embedded
Caplin was restarted a few slots after the fork. Times are UTC.

- Run 28, neither fix, restart at slot 67: the collector flushed blocks
up to #66 and sent #66 as finalized. Caplin then asked the EL to verify
#64 again, and the EL logged `too far unwind. requested=64,
minAllowed=65` 100 times. The EL head stayed at #66 from 23:52:53 to
00:04:54, about 12 minutes, until the checkpoints advanced at slot 128
(justified epoch 3, finalized epoch 2). The node's validator client
failed 11 block proposals in that time.
- Run 30, only the second fix, restart at slot 70: no `too far unwind`.
The collector flushed blocks up to #69 (`Inserting blocks from=1 to=69`)
and sent #69 as finalized. #69 was the payload of the slot 72 block, and
the network made that payload EMPTY: the slot 77 block built on the slot
72 block with #68 as its execution parent. From then on, every
fork-choice update to a block of the network's chain above #68 needed an
unwind below #69, so the EL returned InvalidForkchoice (`forkchoice was
invalid` 834 times). The EL head stayed at #69 until the end of the run,
20 minutes later. The node's beacon API reported justified/finalized 0/0
at slots 100 and 170, when the other nodes reported 2/0 and 4/3, and all
19 block proposals of its validator client after the restart failed.
- Run 31, both fixes, restart at slot 70: no `too far unwind` and no
`forkchoice was invalid`. The EL head caught up with the network about
90 s after the restart, the node reported justified/finalized 4/3 at
slot 170 like the other nodes, and Caplin validators on both Erigon
nodes made all 21 of their proposals in slots 96-169. The restarted
node's validator client failed one proposal, at slot 71, right after the
restart. In this run the collector's last block (#67) stayed canonical,
so the devnet did not exercise the case the first fix handles; its unit
test checks that the collector's fork-choice updates send zero safe and
finalized hashes.

Runs 28 and 30 used main-based builds and run 31 a release/3.7-based
build, all with other open Caplin PRs.

The first fix does not repair a datadir that already holds a false
finalized marker.

Not changed here:
- The EL's shortcut for a fork-choice update whose head is already the
canonical head writes safe and finalized only to the block overlay,
which it does not commit. The markers are stored by the next successful
fork-choice update that moves the head.
- The execution block hash Caplin's fork choice uses for a head block
whose payload is EMPTY.
- `ForkValidator`'s own canonical check.
- The EL still looks up the zero safe and finalized hashes of a
collector fork-choice update before skipping them, which can mean two
failed header lookups per batch.
- The new check gets the finalized block number from
`rawdb.ReadForkchoiceFinalizedNum`, which reads the DB-only
hash-to-number table, and `pruneCanonicalMarkers` deletes entries of
that table below the marker-prune threshold. `unwindIfNeeded` reads the
same marker through the snapshot-aware `blockReader.HeaderNumber`. If
the number is missing, the helper returns 0, so any block above genesis
takes the existing path.

## Changes

-
`cl/phase1/execution_client/block_collector/persistent_block_collector.go`:
`doForkChoiceUpdate` sends zero safe and finalized hashes.
-
`cl/phase1/execution_client/block_collector/persistent_block_collector_test.go`:
the test harness records the safe and finalized hashes of each
fork-choice update; one new test.
- `execution/execmodule/exec_module.go`: the check above, read in the
same transaction (or block overlay) as the header and body, and the
early return after the `MaxReorgDepth` check. The new path creates no
validation domains; on main, the ones created for a canonical block were
not closed.
- `execution/execmodule/exec_module_test.go`: three new tests and one
strengthened test.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestFlushDoesNotClaimSafeOrFinalized` failed before the
collector change, which sent the inserted blocks as finalized.
`TestValidateChainAlreadyCanonicalExecutedAfterPrune` failed before the
`ValidateChain` change with `too far unwind. requested=2, minAllowed=3`:
with `AlwaysGenerateChangesets` off and background pruning, it finalizes
block 4 and validates canonical block 2 after the changesets needed to
unwind to it are pruned. It now gets VALID, and the head, Execution
progress and the validation of the next block are unaffected.
- `TestValidateChainDoesNotTrustCanonicalMarkerAboveFinalized` sets up
the state-ahead recovery, which marks a fork canonical above finalized
block 5 while Execution progress stays at 10, and checks that fork block
8 still takes the existing path. It passes on main and fails without the
finalized bound (VALID instead of `too far unwind`).
- `TestValidateChainCanonicalNotExecutedAfterPrune` has the same setup
as `TestValidateChainAlreadyCanonicalExecutedAfterPrune`, then lowers
the Execution stage progress below block 2 and checks that
`ValidateChain` takes the existing path (`too far unwind`) instead of
returning VALID. It fails when the Execution progress check is replaced
with `return true, nil`, which no other test caught.
- `TestValidateForkPayloadOffNonTipCanonicalBlockWithCache` now
validates the fork blocks one at a time and checks that the first
side-fork block creates an extending fork in `ForkValidator`, as a
control that side-fork blocks still take the existing path.
- `make lint`
- `make erigon integration`
- `go test ./cl/phase1/execution_client/... ./execution/execmodule/...
./execution/engineapi/... ./execution/execfinality/...`

author: lystopad
subject: cl/p2p, cmd: add a QUIC disable switch and default the QUIC port to 4002 (#24443)
body:
Follow-up to #24117.

## Summary

- Add `--caplin.quic.disable` and `--sentinel.quic.disable`. When set:
- the QUIC transport is never registered with libp2p, so no UDP socket
opens at all; the endpoint is not just hidden from the ENR
- the discv5/QUIC port-conflict check and the bind validation in
`NewP2Pmanager` skip QUIC
  - the ENR carries no `quic` or `quic6` entry
- Default `--caplin.discovery.quicport` and `--sentinel.quic.port` to
`4002` instead of `4001`. This matches the usual convention: Lighthouse,
Lodestar, Teku, Nimbus and Grandine all default QUIC to the TCP port
plus one. It also avoids a UDP port collision with discv5 under the
upstream `ethereum-package` Caplin launcher, which starts Caplin with
`--sentinel.tcp.port=4001 --discovery.port=4001`.
- Update the docs and docker-compose examples for the new port default
and the disable switch, and regenerate the `llms-full.txt` artifacts.

## Why

Review on #24117 noted that the other major CL clients ship a TCP-only
switch (Lighthouse `--disable-quic`, Lodestar `--quic=false`, Grandine
`--disable-quic-support`) and Caplin had none: "operators who can't open
a UDP port have no way out."

This matters for Docker and Kubernetes deployments. Exposing an extra
UDP port is often harder than TCP: Services need an explicit `protocol:
UDP`, some managed ingress and load-balancer setups don't forward UDP at
all, and network policies can be stricter. Without a disable switch, the
ENR keeps advertising a `quic` endpoint that such operators can never
make reachable. The switch only helps when the QUIC port specifically
can't be opened: discv5 still needs its UDP port (`4000`), and the docs
say so.

## Connection deduplication: removed, moved to #24538

Earlier iterations of this PR also tried to deduplicate TCP and QUIC
connections to the same peer in the connection gater. go-libp2p does not
deduplicate across transports, so two peers that dial each other at
about the same time can keep two connections. Review showed that every
gater-based approach tried here was worse than keeping the duplicate:

- closing the "newer" or the non-QUIC connection can pick different
survivors on the two sides, and races `cl/sentinel`'s handshake-failure
and ban paths
- rejecting any new connection while one exists leaves zero connections
when two gated nodes dial each other at once, and a dead connection
blocks reconnection

So this PR no longer changes the gater: `InterceptSecured` allows every
connection, as on `main`, and duplicates behave as before this PR. A
deterministic dedup that both sides agree on is tracked in #24538.
Taking it out also lets the switch and the 4002 default go into 3.7.1
together with the QUIC backport (#24413), so 3.7.1 does not ship QUIC on
4001.

## Testing

- `go test -race ./cl/p2p/... ./cl/sentinel/... ./cmd/caplin/...
./cmd/sentinel/... ./cmd/utils/...`: all pass
- `go build ./...` and `make lint`: clean
- Docs: `npm run build` in `docs/site` (Node 20), then `python3
docs/site/scripts/generate-llms.py --check` and `python3 -m unittest
discover docs/site/scripts` (Python 3.11): all pass
- Earlier on this branch: `make erigon integration`, and checked by hand
that `--caplin.quic.disable`, `--sentinel.quic.disable` and the new
`4002` default show up in `--help` for both the `erigon` and `caplin`
binaries

## Scope note

Bounded per-source-IP limiting of connection attempts came up while
discussing this PR, but it is out of scope here. It is a separate
problem (admission control before the handshake, not deduplication by
peer identity), tracked in #24449 (#24448).

author: lystopad
subject: cl/beacon/handler: select block attestations by marginal proposer reward (#24566)
body:
Part of #24554 (point 3). Replaces #24556, closed because its branch
picked up an accidental stacked merge and revert.

## Problem

`findBestAttestationsForBlockProduction` scored every candidate once
against the pre-block state, sorted, and took the top
`MAX_ATTESTATIONS[_ELECTRA]`.
- Overlapping candidates (e.g. the second per-committee layer from
`electraMergedAttestationCandidates`) were credited with votes an
earlier pick already covers. They could push out candidates with fresh
votes.
- Candidates that add nothing after earlier picks were still packed.

## Change

Greedy maximum coverage over the proposer reward, as phase0
`validator.md` asks ("…from the largest number of validators whose
signatures from the same epoch have not previously been added on
chain"):
- After each pick, count only participation flags not set by earlier
picks. Stop once no candidate is worth at least one gwei, the same
threshold as the old zero-reward filter.
- **Lazy greedy:** a candidate's remaining reward only shrinks, so only
the leader of a max-heap is re-scored.
- Ties are broken by signature, so the block does not depend on pool
iteration order.
- **Candidate layout:** per attester, a validator index, base reward and
bitmask of newly set flags (~17 B), with the target epoch on the
candidate. Attesters with no new flag are not stored.
- **Covered flags:** one byte per validator for each epoch.

The reward formula is unchanged (`computeAttestationReward` becomes
`newAttestationCandidate`). Other clients do the same:
- Lighthouse: `maximum_cover` with `update_covering_set`.
- Teku: `RewardBasedAttestationSorter`.
- Prysm: OffchainLabs/prysm#17416.

## Cost

| Benchmark | Time | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| `BenchmarkSelectAttestations`: 32 overlapping candidates of 64×425
validators, mainnet-sized indices, limit 8 | ~5 ms | ~4 MB (covered
flags) |
| `BenchmarkSelectAttestationsManyDisjoint`: pre-Electra shape, 2048
candidates, limit 128 | ~4 ms | — |

A full mainnet candidate takes ~0.46 MB.

## Tests

- `TestSelectAttestations*`:
  - skips votes already covered,
  - drops candidates without new reward,
  - counts new flags of covered validators,
  - tracks epochs separately,
  - drops candidates worth < 1 gwei with the real denominator,
  - breaks ties independently of input order,
  - keeps epoch flags apart for any flag count.
- `TestNewAttestationCandidate*`: only new flags recorded, base reward
from effective balance, previous-epoch participation read, Gloas parent
header slot.
- I checked that the coverage tests fail when the corresponding logic is
broken.

Not covered: an end-to-end `findBestAttestationsForBlockProduction` test
(needs a full state fixture). The proposer reward denominator is still
duplicated with `processAttestationPostAltair`; unifying them would
touch state-transition code, so it is left out of this PR.

`go test ./cl/beacon/...` passes, and `make lint` reports 0 issues on 2
runs.

author: lystopad
subject: cl/beacon/handler: aggregate PTC votes after the payload wait (#24662)
body:
Fixes #24661.

## Problem

Blocks proposed by Caplin on Sepolia carry noticeably fewer PTC votes
than blocks from other clients. Measured over 296 recent slots:
Caplin-proposed blocks average 444/512 set bits in
`payload_attestations` (median 433), other proposers 504/512 (median
511).

`produceBeaconBody` aggregated the PTC votes for the parent slot from
the epbs pool in a goroutine started at the beginning of production,
4–47 ms into the slot (`aggregatePayloadAttestations took` is logged at
`.041`), while the block is only assembled after the execution payload
wait, ~0.65 s into the slot with a prepared payload and ~2.2 s
otherwise. PTC votes are due at 75% of the parent slot, but a tail of
them arrives around the slot boundary (gossip accepts a
`payload_attestation_message` up to `MAXIMUM_GOSSIP_CLOCK_DISPARITY`
into the next slot), so the early snapshot missed them. Clients that
aggregate when they assemble the block include them.

## Change

Aggregate the PTC votes after the payload wait, right before the body is
finalised. The aggregation takes ~40 ms on Sepolia, inside the
publication margin production already reserves. The slot and root used
for the aggregation are unchanged (`targetSlot-1`, parent root).

## Testing

- `go test ./cl/beacon/handler/`, `make lint`.
- Placement-only change with no new logic; the existing production tests
cover the aggregation itself. TDD skipped for that reason. The effect is
measurable on a live node by counting the set bits of
`payload_attestations[].aggregation_bits` in Caplin-proposed blocks; the
expected value after the change is close to 511/512, as for other
clients.

author: lystopad
subject: cl/phase1/network/services: read same-epoch parent state in place for gossip block validation (#24523)
body:
Fixes #24522

## Problem

`computeBlockValidationContext` copied the full parent beacon state and
ran `ProcessSlots` on it for every gossip block. It only needs three
values from that state: the expected proposer, the latest block hash and
the latest bid. On mainnet this adds ~0.4s per block before the block
can become head. That is enough to push about 11% of slots past the 4s
sync committee and attestation deadline. Measurements are in the issue.

## Change

Epoch processing and fork upgrades run only at epoch boundaries. So
advancing the parent state to a slot in its own epoch cannot change any
of the values read here. In that case (31 of 32 blocks), the context is
now read from the parent state in place via `ViewStateAtBlockRoot`.
Blocks that cross an epoch boundary keep the copy + `ProcessSlots` path,
so fork upgrades (including the Gloas upgrade that rewrites the latest
bid and block hash) stay handled.

The rule does not depend on fork-specific dependent roots, so it works
on every network and fork. Prysm, Teku and Lodestar use the same
approach.

## Tests

- New `TestBlockValidationContextReadsSameEpochParentStateWithoutCopy`
failed before the fix: it requested a copied parent state.
- New `TestBlockValidationContextAdvancesCopiedParentStateAcrossEpoch`
guards the epoch-crossing path. It also passes without the fix, as
expected for a guard.
- In `TestBlockServiceGossipRejectsUnexpectedProposer` and
`TestBlockServiceUnrelatedReservationDoesNotRevalidateP2P`, the stubs
required copied parent-state reads. They now also serve read-only views.
Their real assertions are unchanged: one shared parent-state read under
concurrency, and a single validation call.

`go test ./cl/phase1/network/services/` passes, and `make lint` reports
0 issues (2 runs).

The backport to `release/3.7` will follow after merge.

author: lystopad
subject: cl/antiquary: retire one blob segment per attempt (#24586)
body:
Fixes #24314.

## Problem

`antiquateBlobs` dumps the whole pending blob backlog in one
`DumpBlobsSidecar` call, and opens the snapshot folder, seeds and prunes
only after the last segment is written. During a catch-up, for example
the 72-segment Sepolia backlog in the issue that took more than 8 hours:

- `frozen_blobs` stays still for the whole run and then jumps, so a
working dump looks the same as a wedged one;
- `frozen_blocks` stops too, because block retirement runs in the same
retirement tick and waits behind the call;
- blob sidecars stay in the database until the very end;
- a failure on a late segment throws away all earlier work: those
segment files are on disk but not opened, so the next attempt restarts
from the old frontier.

## Change

Dump only the next segment per attempt. The rest of `antiquateBlobs` is
unchanged, and now runs per segment:

- the folder is reopened after each segment, so the existing
`frozen_blobs` gauge advances by one segment (10,000 slots) at a time;
no new metric is needed;
- block retirement runs between segments;
- each segment is seeded and pruned from the database as soon as it is
written;
- a failure loses at most one segment, since earlier segments are
already visible and the next attempt resumes after them;
- the start log names the backlog end: `Antiquating blobs from=… to=…
backlogTo=…`.

Compression parallelism is still decided from the whole backlog
(`isBlobBacklog`), so a catch-up keeps the workers #24316 gave it.

The range checks move into `nextBlobSegment`. It returns `to = from +
CaplinMergeLimit`, and `DumpBlobsSidecar` dumps exactly one segment for
that range. The existing `to = (to / CaplinMergeLimit) *
CaplinMergeLimit` line still gives the end of what was dumped, so
seeding and pruning never cover slots that were not written. A redundant
check (`frozenBlobs >= frozenBlocks`, implied by the one that follows)
is dropped; a mutation test showed it had no effect.

## Blob retirement no longer trails block retirement by a segment

The range check compared `FrozenBlobs()`, the exclusive end of the last
blob segment, with `BlocksAvailable()`, the last frozen block slot (the
block segment's end minus one). With block segments frozen through slot
11,249,999, the blob segment `[11,240,000, 11,250,000)` has every block
it needs but was refused, so blob retirement always trailed block
retirement by one whole segment: about 33 hours on mainnet and 14 hours
on Gnosis. The backlog end was one slot short as well, so a backlog of
exactly two segments was classed as tip work and compressed on one
worker.

`nextBlobSegment` now reads the block frontier with
`VisibleSegmentsMaxTo(BeaconBlocks)`, the accessor `FrozenBlobs()` is
built on, so both frontiers are exclusive segment ends. This predates
this PR; it is fixed here because `nextBlobSegment` is the code this PR
rewrites, and its first version carried the bug into a test case.

Checked for side effects:

- Blob coverage up to, but not past, the block end is what the rest of
the code expects. The beacon API serves `slot < FrozenBlobs()` from
snapshots. The blob downloader uses `FrozenBlobs()` as its floor.
`db/integrity`'s coverage check rejects only blob segments ending past
the block end. Caplin snapshots are not `alignMin`, so no type's
segments are hidden for another's coverage.
- No chain-specific behaviour changes. Every supported chain configures
Deneb (mainnet, Sepolia, Hoodi, Gnosis, Chiado, bloatnet), Caplin's
merge limit is 10,000 slots on all of them, and the Deneb floor and
`SlotsPerEpoch` are handled as before.
- One visible effect: when caught up, `frozen_blocks` (inclusive) now
reads one less than `frozen_blobs` (exclusive), instead of 9,999 more. A
panel of `frozen_blocks - frozen_blobs` shows −1 rather than 9,999 at
the tip.

## Flags

No flag changes when blob retirement runs. `--caplin.snapgen=false`
still returns before any of this, and the `--caplin.blobs-archive` /
`--caplin.blobs-immediate-backfill` backfill gate is unchanged. At the
chain tip, where the backlog is a single segment, the behaviour is the
same as before.

## Not addressed

The issue also notes that `progress`/`eta` on the
`[BlobHistoryDownloader] Downloading blobs backwards` log are computed
to the Deneb fork while the loop stops at `FrozenBlobs()`. That lives in
`cl/phase1/network/blob_downloader.go`, which #24585 also changes, so it
is left for a follow-up once #24585 lands.

## Tests

- `TestNextBlobSegment`, against a fake that models where the last blob
and block segments end: no work when caught up, blocks short of a whole
segment, a frozen block segment makes its blob segment retirable at
once, a backlog retires only its first segment, the Deneb floor when no
blob segments exist.
- `TestNextBlobSegmentKeepsTheBacklogForCompressionParallelism`: two
pending segments are a catch-up, judged by the backlog end rather than
the segment end.

`TestNextBlobSegment` was written first and failed for the intended
reason against a stub that kept the old whole-backlog behaviour. The
parallelism test pins a contract the helper already met, so it passed on
its first run; the mutations below show it is not vacuous. Each of these
fails a test: dumping the whole backlog per attempt, losing the backlog
end, dropping the Deneb floor, an off-by-one in either direction on the
segment check.

For the off-by-one fix, the test was rewritten first to take real
segment ends, and failed as expected: the complete segment was refused
and the backlog end was one slot short. Each of these also fails it:
reading the blob segment end as the block frontier, and going back to an
inclusive block frontier.

`antiquateBlobs` itself has no test harness (it needs real snapshots, a
database and blob storage), so the call-site wiring is covered by review
rather than by a test.

`make lint` (repeated), `make erigon integration`, and `go test -race`
for `cl/antiquary/...`, `cl/phase1/stages/...` and
`db/snapshotsync/freezeblocks/...` pass.

author: fmtappendf
subject: cl/aggregation: avoid uint64 underflow when checking stale slots (#24652)
body:
`cl/aggregation/pool_impl.go` `slotIsStale` subtracted two `uint64`
slots without checking ordering:

	curSlot - targetSlot > p.netConfig.AttestationPropagationSlotRange

When `targetSlot > curSlot` (a future/current slot) the subtraction
underflows to ~2^64, which is always
`> AttestationPropagationSlotRange` (default 32), so the function
returns `true` and valid future
attestations are dropped from the aggregation pool.



Guard the subtraction so a future/current slot is never reported stale,
mirroring the existing helper in
`cl/validator/committee_subscription/committee_subscription.go`:

	if curSlot <= targetSlot {
		// Avoid subtracting unsigned integers
		return false
	}
	return curSlot-targetSlot > p.netConfig.AttestationPropagationSlotRange

The identical guard (with the comment `// Avoid subtracting unsigned
integers`) already exists in
`cl/validator/committee_subscription/committee_subscription.go`, so this
aligns the aggregation pool
with the project's own established pattern.

author: Chase Wright
subject: cl/utils/eth_clock: keep ENR next_fork_version at a BPO fork (#24406)
body:
`ForkId()` takes `next_fork_version` from the next *regular* fork.
`next_fork_epoch` comes from `NextForkEpochIncludeBPO()`, which also
counts BPO forks. When a BPO fork is scheduled before the next regular
fork, the two halves of the `eth2` value describe different forks: the
version of the regular fork and the epoch of the BPO fork.

The [Fulu p2p
spec](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/blob/82b6e507dc31f6f7052e79b16ecfe3778c1b38f6/specs/fulu/p2p-interface.md#eth2-field)
says:

> `next_fork_version` is the fork version corresponding to the next
planned fork at a future epoch. The fork version will only change for
regular forks, _not BPO forks_. Note that it is possible for the blob
schedule to define a change at the same epoch as a regular fork; this
situation would be considered a regular fork. If no future fork is
planned, set `next_fork_version = current_fork_version` to signal this
fact.

This PR sets `next_fork_version` to the version in effect at
`next_fork_epoch`. If no fork is scheduled, it is the current version.
Nimbus uses the same rule
(`forkVersionAtEpoch(nextForkEpochAtEpoch(epoch))`).

Example: the current fork is Fulu, with a BPO fork at epoch A and Gloas
at epoch B > A.

| | next_fork_version | next_fork_epoch |
|---|---|---|
| before | Gloas | A |
| after | Fulu | A |

`ForkId()` now derives all three fields from one epoch sample. Before,
it sampled the epoch three times, so an epoch boundary between samples
could give a mismatched triple that `updateENR` only repairs at the next
fork.

### Why this matters for peering

Prysm's discv5 dial filter (`compareForkENR` in
`beacon-chain/p2p/fork.go`, called from `filterPeer`, since
OffchainLabs/prysm#15604) handles a peer whose current fork digest
matches as follows:

- If `next_fork_epoch` differs, it allows the dial.
- If `next_fork_epoch` matches and is not `FAR_FUTURE_EPOCH`, it rejects
the peer when `next_fork_version` differs.

Prysm gives BPO entries the version of the last regular fork. While the
epoch was big-endian, Caplin's epoch never matched while a fork was
scheduled, so Prysm always took the first branch. After #24405, the
epochs match, and Prysm reaches the version comparison. In the window
described above, Prysm would then not dial Caplin nodes that it finds
through discovery. So #24405 makes this change necessary before the next
network schedules a BPO fork before a regular fork.

<details><summary>Client survey (default branches, 2026-09-29)</summary>

`next_fork_version` when a BPO fork is scheduled before the next regular
fork:

| client | next_fork_version | next_fork_epoch |
|---|---|---|
| Prysm | current | BPO |
| Lodestar | current | BPO |
| Nimbus | current | BPO |
| Lighthouse | next regular fork | BPO |
| Teku | next regular fork | BPO |
| Grandine | next regular fork | next regular fork |
| Caplin (before) | next regular fork | BPO |
| Caplin (after) | current | BPO |

Lighthouse and Teku have the same behavior as Caplin had before this PR.
The clients disagree, so the spec could state this rule more explicitly
(ethereum/consensus-specs#5701). This PR follows the spec text as it is
written now.
</details>

No public network is in this state today. On mainnet and Hoodi, no
regular fork is scheduled after their BPOs. On Sepolia, both BPO forks
are in the past and only Gloas (epoch 353024) is ahead.

`TestForkIdNextForkVersionWithBPO` covers four cases: a BPO before
Gloas, a BPO at the same epoch as Gloas, Gloas before a BPO, and a BPO
with no Gloas scheduled. It checks the encoded version and epoch bytes.
Before this change, only "bpo before gloas" fails (`expected:
0x0600006f, actual: 0x0700006f`). The test sets genesis relative to
`time.Now()` and uses its own blob schedule, so it does not depend on
the date or on Chiado's live schedule.

When two regular forks share one future epoch, `next_fork_version` is
now the later fork (before: the earlier one). This is
`compute_fork_version(next_fork_epoch)`, the version from which peers
compute the digest at that epoch.
`TestForkIdNextForkVersionWithForksAtSameEpoch` covers it and fails
before this change. Only devnet or custom configs can reach this state.

author: lystopad
subject: cl/phase1/network: say why blob backfill is incomplete, and export its state (#24585)
body:
Fixes #24113.

## Problem

Blob retirement (`retirementTick` in `cl/antiquary`) waits until the
blob history backfill reports complete. When it doesn't, the only signal
is the periodic `[BlobHistoryDownloader] Blob backfilling is not
finished, some blobs might be unavailable` warning, which names only
`currentSlot` and `highestBackfilled`. From that, an operator cannot
tell:

- how far blob snapshots have fallen behind block snapshots, and
- which slots keep the backfill from completing: a pass still in
progress, or a gap that will never fill (for example, older than the
serve window on an archive node).

There is no metric for the backfill state at all.

The issue describes the gate as completely silent. That was true on the
node it was observed on: before #23895 the backfill pass never finished,
and this warning shares a goroutine with the pass, so it never fired. On
`main` the pass finishes and the warning does fire, so this PR extends
it rather than adding a second warning for the same condition.

## Change

- **New fields on the existing warning:**
- `frozenBlobsTo` and `frozenBlocksTo`: the blob and block snapshot
frontiers, both as exclusive segment ends (the block end is read with
`VisibleSegmentsMaxTo(BeaconBlocks)`), so caught-up snapshots show the
same value and the unfrozen range is their plain difference;
- `unresolvedSlots`, `lowestUnresolved` and `highestUnresolved`: a
summary of the retry ranges, when there are any.
- **New gauge `caplin_blob_backfill_complete` (0/1):** published when
the downloader starts, then set in `setBackfillCompleted`, where the
downloader decides completion. So an enabled downloader exports 0 from
the start, including during a long first pass or while it waits for
peers or sync. It is created then rather than at package init, so nodes
that never run blob backfill do not export a 0 that would read as a
stall.

The message text is unchanged, so existing log-based alerts keep
matching. `blobSnapshotReader` gains `VisibleSegmentsMaxTo()`, which
`CaplinSnapshots` already implements.

## When the warning and the gauge appear

| Configuration | Blob downloader runs | Warning |
`caplin_blob_backfill_complete` |
|---|---|---|---|
| default flags | no (`Start()` is a no-op) | never | not exported |
| `--caplin.blobs-archive` | yes, after block backfill finishes | every
4 min while incomplete (unchanged cadence) | exported from downloader
start |
| `--caplin.blobs-immediate-backfill` | yes, within the serve window |
every 4 min while incomplete | exported from downloader start |
| `--caplin.use-engine-api` | `ArchiveBlobs` is forced off; immediate
backfill is still read | as above for immediate backfill | as above |
| `--caplin.snapgen=false` | unaffected | unaffected; the frontiers come
from downloaded snapshots | unaffected |
| no Caplin (external CL) | no | never | not exported |

One pre-existing inconsistency, left out of scope: with
`--caplin.use-engine-api`, `setCaplin` warns that immediate blob
backfilling is disabled but still reads the flag.

## Tests

- `TestSetBackfillCompletedSetsCompletionGauge`: the gauge follows
completion, including when completion is revoked.
- `TestFirstRetrySlotExportsIncompleteBackfill`: the first report on a
fresh downloader, an unchanged false, still writes the gauge.
- `TestStartExportsBackfillStateBeforeTheFirstPass` /
`TestStartWithoutBlobBackfillLeavesTheGaugeAlone`: an enabled downloader
publishes the gauge before its first pass, and a disabled one does not
touch it.
- `TestWarnBackfillIncompleteNamesFrontiersAndUnresolvedSlots` /
`TestWarnBackfillIncompleteWithoutUnresolvedSlots`: the exact log
context, with and without unresolved slots, read from a fake with
distinct blob and block segment ends.

The tests were written first and failed for the intended reason before
the implementation. Each of these mutations also fails a test: gauge
never set to 1, gauge never cleared, lowest unresolved slot taken from
the wrong end, counting ranges instead of slots, frontiers dropped. For
the review follow-up (38daa30dbc): the gauge written after the
unchanged-value early return, no publish at downloader start, a disabled
downloader publishing, the two frontiers swapped, and the blob end read
as the block end.

`make lint` (repeated), `make erigon integration`, and `go test -race`
for `cl/phase1/network/...`, `cl/phase1/stages/...`, `cl/antiquary/...`
and `cl/beacon/handler/...` pass.

author: lystopad
subject: cl: follow the spec's gossip slot window for current and future slots (#24489)
body:
Fixes #24360.

## Problem

`EthereumClock.IsSlotCurrentSlotWithMaximumClockDisparity` is the gossip
slot-window check for sync-committee messages, sync contributions,
blocks, blob sidecars, data column sidecars and pending payload
envelopes. It had three defects.

1. **Overflow.** It computed `genesis + SECONDS_PER_SLOT * slot` without
bounds. With 12-second slots that product repeats every 2^62 slots, so
`current_slot + k·2^62` (k = 1, 2, 3) mapped to the current slot and
passed the check. The sync-committee message signature does not cover
the slot, so a replayed message with such a slot passed the `[IGNORE]`
check, entered the pool and was forwarded.
2. **Wrong window.** It applied `MAXIMUM_GOSSIP_CLOCK_DISPARITY` around
the message slot's start instead of around the current time. In slot N
it therefore:
- accepted messages for slot N+1 during the whole slot, not only in its
last 500 ms
- rejected messages for slot N-1 in the first 500 ms of slot N, which
the spec allows

The spec's `is_current_slot` is `[start(slot) - D, start(slot + 1) + D]`
around the current time. Lighthouse checks the same `now ± D` range.
3. **Late blocks were ignored.** The block gossip check compared the
block slot with the head slot, not the wall-clock slot. When a block for
slot N-1 arrived more than 500 ms into slot N, and the head was still at
N-2, the block was ignored as "from a future slot". It was not scheduled
or forwarded, so the node attested to the older head. The spec's rule is
`is_future_slot`, which compares with the current time only.

## Fix

- `IsSlotCurrentSlotWithMaximumClockDisparity` now implements
`is_current_slot`, inclusive at both ends. It first rejects any slot
that is not the current slot or one of its neighbours. The disparity is
shorter than a slot, so no other slot can qualify, and the time
arithmetic then only runs for slots near the present and cannot
overflow. The clock is read once per check.
- `blockService.validateGossip` compares with
`ethClock.GetCurrentSlot()`. The ignore message now gives the block slot
first: `block is from a future slot: <slot> > <current>`.
- Late blocks now reach the proposer signature check before the
unknown-parent check, and the head state can predate the proposer (for
example right after the forward-sync handoff). Then
`ValidatorForValidatorIndex` fails with `ErrInvalidValidatorIndex`,
which rejected the block and banned the sender. Only the parent's state
is sure to know the proposer, so while the parent is unknown,
`validateGossip` returns `ErrIgnore` and does not schedule the
unverified block. With a known parent, and for any other signature error
such as a malformed signature, the block is still rejected.
- `verifySyncCommitteeMessageSignature` and
`verifySyncContributionProofAggregatedSignature` take the signing domain
from the epoch of the message slot, as the spec does, not from the head
state's epoch. Because previous-slot messages are now accepted for 500
ms, the head state can already be in a new fork while the message slot
is still in the old one. The old code then failed the signature check
and banned the peer that sent the message.
- No other caller changes. The sidecar and payload-envelope callers only
reach the check for a slot ahead of the wall-clock slot, and for such a
slot the fixed predicate is `!is_future_slot`.

Behaviour changes, all towards the spec:
- Messages and sidecars for the next slot are now ignored until 500 ms
before that slot starts. Before, they were accepted and forwarded during
the whole of the previous slot. Spec-following peers already ignore
them, and an ignore does not lower peer score. A node whose clock is
more than 500 ms behind the network now ignores such early blocks and
sidecars instead of queuing them.
- Sync-committee messages and contributions for the previous slot are
accepted for 500 ms after it ends.
- Late blocks for a past slot are no longer ignored when the head is
behind them.
- A pending execution payload envelope for the next slot is retried only
within 500 ms before that slot starts.

The node's own publishing is unaffected. Sync-committee messages go out
about 4 s into the slot and contributions about 8 s in, and blocks and
sidecars after the slot starts.

`GetSlotTime` and `GetSlotByTime` keep their unchecked arithmetic. No
gossip-supplied slot reaches them unbounded: most callers take slots
from the node's own state, the sync-committee publish path is already
bounded, and the payload-attestation check
(`isPayloadAttestationSlotCurrent`) bounds its gossip slot itself. The
one unbounded input is the validator client's `until_epoch` in the
subnet subscription endpoint, where an overflow can only produce a wrong
subscription expiry.

## Tests

- `cl/utils/eth_clock/current_slot_window_test.go`, with an injected
current time:
- the window at millisecond edges: the next slot exactly one disparity
before it starts, and 1 ms earlier; the previous slot exactly one
disparity after it ends, and 1 ms later; slots two ahead and two behind
  - the slots `current + k·2^62` and `MaxUint64` are rejected
  - slot 0 at genesis
- `TestSyncCommitteesIgnoresForgedSlotThatAliasesToNow`: through the
real sync-committee service and the real clock, a message for `current +
2^62` is ignored before any signature verification.
- `TestBlockServiceDoesNotIgnoreLateBlockAsFuture`: with the head behind
and the wall clock past the block's slot, the block passes the slot
check and reaches the signature check (`ErrInvalidSignature`). Before
the fix it was ignored as a block from a future slot.
- `TestBlockServiceIgnoresUnknownProposerWhileParentIsUnknown`,
`TestBlockServiceRejectsUnknownProposerWhenParentIsKnown` and
`TestBlockServiceRejectsMalformedSignatureWhileParentIsUnknown`: a late
block whose proposer is past the head state's registry is ignored and
not scheduled while its parent is unknown, and rejected once the parent
is known; a malformed signature is rejected either way. The first failed
before the fix with `invalid validator index`.
- `TestVerifySyncCommitteeMessageSignatureUsesMessageSlotDomain` and
`TestVerifySyncContributionAggregatedSignatureUsesContributionSlotDomain`:
with the head state at the first slot of a new fork, a message for the
previous slot is verified with the previous fork version. Before the fix
the signing root did not match.

Each was checked by mutation, and each of these mutations fails a test:
- restoring the old implementation
- removing the neighbour bound
- dropping the disparity at either end
- a strict comparison at either end
- excluding the previous slot from the bound
- comparing the block with the head slot again

`go test -race ./cl/...`, the CL spec tests with `-tags=spectest`
(including 272 fork-choice tests), `go build ./...`, `make lint` and
`make lintci` pass.

After the second commit, `make lint`, `make erigon integration` and the
tests of `cl/phase1/network/services`, `cl/utils/eth_clock` and
`cl/beacon/handler` pass.

After the review follow-up (merge of main, bcd19c9a3a, 0a2385c805),
`make lint`, `make erigon integration` and `go test -race` for
`cl/utils/eth_clock/...`, `cl/phase1/network/...`,
`cl/beacon/handler/...` and `cl/phase1/stages/...` pass. Each of these
mutations of the late-block fix fails a test: no ignore path, ignoring
with a known parent, scheduling the unverified block, and ignoring any
signature error while the parent is unknown.

The fork-domain case where the head lags behind a new fork is
pre-existing and tracked in #24689.

author: Andrew Ashikhmin
subject: cl: cap inferred SSZ committee bits width and reject oversized custom presets (#24614)
body:
## Summary

Cap config-less Electra and later `Attestation` SSZ decoding at the
widest supported preset: 64 committees, or 8 bytes of `committee_bits`.
Reject a wider inferred vector before allocation. All nested SSZ paths
share this check, including aggregates, block bodies, and beacon API SSZ
requests. Config-aware decoding still requires the exact configured
width.

`CustomConfig` now rejects `MAX_COMMITTEES_PER_SLOT > 64` while loading
the file. The loader and decoder use the same supported limit, so
incompatible custom configurations fail at startup instead of later
rejecting aggregates, blocks, and stored data.

## Compatibility

- Built-in presets are unchanged: mainnet uses 64 committees and minimal
uses 4.
- Custom presets above 64 were partly supported before this change when
their aggregation bitlists stayed below the old limit. They are now
explicitly rejected during configuration loading.
- JSON decoding is unchanged. `ValidateForConfig` checks the committee
vector width after JSON decoding.
- `NewBitVector` remains unchanged. Other types use larger vectors;
`PayloadAttestation` infers its vector width from the input slice, whose
element size is bounded by the configured preset in block bodies.

author: Andrew Ashikhmin
subject: cl: reject negative validator indices in state accessors (#24615)
body:
SSZ validator indices are `uint64` and are converted with `int()` before
they reach the per-validator accessors of `raw.BeaconState`. Those
accessors only checked the upper bound, so a converted value `>= 2^63`
passed the guard as a negative index and reached the slice arithmetic in
`solid.ValidatorSet` and the byte-backed uint64 slice. Depending on the
value, that was a runtime panic or, when the multiplication by the
element size wrapped around, a silent read or write of the wrong
element.

Changes:

- All error-returning per-validator getters and setters of
`raw.BeaconState` return `ErrInvalidValidatorIndex` for a negative
index: 27 existing guards were made two-sided, and the five setters that
had no bounds check gained one.
- `solid.ValidatorSet` treats a negative index as out of bounds in
`Get`, `Set` and the internal phase0 and attester-bit accessors.
- The byte-backed uint64 slice (balances, inactivity scores) rejects
negative indices in `Get` and gains the missing bounds check in `Set`.

All non-test call sites that convert a `uint64` index to `int` before
calling `ValidatorForValidatorIndex` go through the shared guard, so no
call site needed changing. In particular `VerifyBlockSignature` now
returns `ErrInvalidValidatorIndex` for a proposer index `>= 2^63`
instead of panicking.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/forkchoice: keep Fulu blocks out of fork choice until their custody columns are stored (#24546)
body:
## Summary

Fulu fork choice admits a block only when its data is available
(`is_data_available` in `on_block`). Caplin checked custody columns but,
on a node that was not syncing, only scheduled a deferred download and
admitted the block anyway. When the EL reported the blobs it skipped the
check without storing any columns. The node then attested to and
advertised a block while holding part of its custody columns.

In a devnet Lighthouse requested those columns from Caplin, got short
answers (1 of 5, 1 of 3, 2 of 8 columns), scored each -10
(`NotEnoughResponsesReturned`) and banned Caplin within six minutes of
genesis.

`on_block` now returns `ErrEIP7594ColumnDataNotAvailable` whenever the
custody columns are missing; the gossip block queue retries such a block
every 50 ms for up to 30 s. The EL blob shortcut is used only before
Fulu. Gloas is unchanged: its data availability is checked on the
envelope.

The shortcut fired far more often than intended on Erigon with embedded
Caplin: the local txpool returns an entry for every requested hash,
empty when it does not have the blob, so the length check always passed
and embedded nodes admitted every Fulu gossip block without checking
columns.

Chain tip and forward sync import blocks with the availability check
disabled, as before, so this does not stall the node: if the columns are
still missing after about half a slot, chain tip sync fetches the block
and imports it without them (6.1-6.5 s in the devnet). The change
narrows the window in which the node attests to and advertises a block
it cannot serve; it does not close it.

Cost: from Fulu a block is no longer admitted on EL blobs, and Caplin
cannot build columns from them, so admission waits for gossip custody
columns (or reconstruction on a supernode). For embedded nodes this
replaces no wait at all. When columns arrive more than about 4 s into
the slot, the node attests to the parent and loses the head vote. In the
devnet, gossip admission took 0.09-1.1 s at the median, but this has not
been measured on mainnet; a canary on an embedded mainnet node
(admission latency, chain tip fallbacks, head-vote accuracy) is
advisable before merging. Building custody columns from
`engine_getBlobsV2` would remove the cost and is left for a follow-up.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/on_block.go`: the pre-Gloas availability check
moves into `checkPreGloasBlockDataAvailability`, which fails closed for
Fulu.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/block_data_availability_test.go`: new test.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestPreGloasBlockDataAvailabilityRequiresFuluCustodyColumns`
failed against main's availability logic placed in the new helper (two

- Devnet (setup below): Lighthouse logged no
`NotEnoughResponsesReturned` against Caplin.
- `make lint`

Devnet used below: a local Kurtosis network with Lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0

author: Kewei
subject: cl: use the Fulu inclusion proof depth for data column sidecars (#24512)
body:
## Summary

When Caplin publishes a Fulu block with blobs,
`broadcastBlockWithIntegrationWaitAndPublication` builds the data column
sidecars. This helper builds the sidecars of the full blocks Caplin
publishes for its validators; Fulu blinded blocks are published by the
relay, not by Caplin. It creates the `kzg_commitments_inclusion_proof`
vector with `cltypes.CommitmentBranchSize` (17, the Deneb `BlobSidecar`
depth) instead of `cltypes.KzgCommitmentsInclusionProofDepth` (4,
`KZG_COMMITMENTS_INCLUSION_PROOF_DEPTH` in the Fulu spec). The first 4
hashes are the real proof, the other 13 are zero.

`DataColumnSidecar` encodes this field as a fixed vector of whatever
length it holds, so the SSZ fixed part is 772 bytes instead of 356.
Spec-conformant decoders reject it. The same sidecars are gossiped and
written to storage, and the req/resp handlers serve the stored bytes.

On a local Kurtosis devnet (Lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0, Teku 26.9.1, Caplin
v3.7.1):
- Lighthouse logged `Could not decode gossipsub message ...
OffsetSkipsVariableBytes(772)` on all 128 `data_column_sidecar_N` topics
for the first Caplin block with blobs.
- A Lighthouse `data_columns_by_root` request to a Caplin peer failed
with `SSZDecodeError(OffsetSkipsVariableBytes(772))`. Lighthouse treats
this as a fatal peer action and banned the Caplin node.

With this change, in the same setup Lighthouse logged no
`OffsetSkipsVariableBytes` errors and verified the columns of Caplin's
blocks, and Lighthouse and both Caplin nodes had the same block roots
for slots 60-75, across the Gloas fork at slot 64.

Caplin's own decoder reads the first 4 hashes and does not check the
first offset, so Caplin peers accept these sidecars. The existing test
decodes with Caplin and passed before this change.

Scope: Fulu blocks with blobs published by Caplin. Gloas sidecars have
no inclusion proof and use another code path. The columns of blocks a
node published before upgrading are also stored with the 17-hash proof
(received columns are decoded with the 4-hash proof and stored that
way), and req/resp served the stored bytes as they are. The second and
third commits fix this: when serving a stored pre-Gloas column,
`WriteStream` reads only the length prefix of the file, and only if the
declared SSZ length matches the 17-hash layout it decodes the sidecar
(Caplin's decoder reads the first 4 hashes) and encodes it again. Other
pre-Gloas files are copied raw after that prefix read, and Gloas files
are copied raw without it, as before. So an upgraded node stops sending
undecodable sidecars right away instead of after they are pruned,
without decoding the columns that are already canonical. The vector size
comes from #16083 (2025-07). `release/3.7` has the same code.

## Changes

- `cl/beacon/handler/block_production.go`: size the Fulu inclusion proof
vector with `KzgCommitmentsInclusionProofDepth`.
- `cl/beacon/handler/block_production_request_blobs_test.go`:
`TestPostEthV2BeaconBlocksPublishesRequestColumnsOnNonProducingNode` now
also checks that each published column is the canonical SSZ encoding
(decode, re-encode, compare the bytes).
- `cl/persistence/blob_storage/data_column_db.go`: `WriteStream`
re-encodes a stored pre-Gloas file whose length matches the 17-hash
layout and copies every other file raw. It reads the uncompressed SSZ
length from the prefix: the fixed part of a Fulu `DataColumnSidecar` is
356 bytes with the 4-hash proof and 772 with the 17-hash one, and each
blob adds 2144 bytes (a cell, a commitment and a proof), so for a valid
sidecar `length % 2144 == 772` holds for the 17-hash layout and never
for the canonical one, for any number of blobs.
- `cl/persistence/blob_storage/data_column_db_test.go`:
`TestWriteStreamServesLegacyInclusionProofCanonically` (a column stored
with the 17-hash proof is served with the 4-hash proof) and
`TestWriteStreamServesCanonicalFileVerbatim` (a canonical file with one
junk byte appended is served byte for byte, so it is not decoded).

## Testing

- **TDD:** before the fix, the extended test failed on the
canonical-encoding check (`column N must use the spec SSZ layout`).
- **TDD:** `TestWriteStreamServesLegacyInclusionProofCanonically` failed
before the second commit.
- **TDD:** `TestWriteStreamServesCanonicalFileVerbatim` failed before
the third commit (the re-encode dropped the junk byte).
- `make lint`
- `make erigon integration`
- `go test ./cl/persistence/... ./cl/sentinel/...
./cl/beacon/handler/...`

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/forkchoice: ignore ticks before genesis (#24680)
body:
## Summary

A Caplin node whose fork choice ticker calls `OnTick` with a pre-genesis
Unix time keeps about one CPU core busy until it is restarted.

During startup Caplin starts a goroutine with a 2 ms ticker that calls
`ForkChoiceStore.OnTick` with the current Unix time
(`cmd/caplin/caplin1/run.go`). `OnTick` computes `tickSlot := (time -
f.genesisTime) / SecondsPerSlot` in uint64. Before genesis the
subtraction wraps, giving about 1.5e18 slots with 12 s slots, and the
catch-up loop advances the store's time one slot per iteration, taking
`f.mu` in each. The first pre-genesis call effectively never returns.
Meanwhile it pushes the store's time far ahead, and either of the other
two production callers can set it back to the start of the current slot.

`OnTick` now returns early when the time is before genesis, which is
outside the spec's `on_tick` domain. Behaviour at and after genesis is
unchanged. The other two production callers derive the time from
`ethClock`, which returns slot 0 before genesis, so the ticker is the
only production caller that can pass a pre-genesis time.

The trigger is a ticker call while the wall clock is before the
configured genesis. This mainly happens on devnets and new network
launches; ordinary starts on live networks such as Mainnet, Sepolia and
Hoodi are not affected.

Devnet: Kurtosis, Fulu at genesis, Gloas at epoch 2, 12 s slots.
- Across 11 of our 6-client runs (44 `docker stats` samples), the
standalone Caplin node, started before genesis and never restarted,
never dropped below 98.75% CPU (median 100%). The other consensus
clients had medians of 0.9-3.1%, with occasional spikes. The Erigon node
with embedded Caplin, which the test harness restarts after genesis, was
at 100-108% in the first sample of every run and mostly much lower
later.
- A 30 s CPU profile of the standalone node, taken after genesis,
attributed 97% of samples cumulatively to `OnTick` (94% to
`onTickPerSlot` within it). A goroutine dump taken after genesis showed
the first `OnTick` call, with a time before genesis, still running.
- Pristine `erigontech/erigon:v3.7.1` as standalone Caplin did the same:
about 100% before and after genesis.
- After a restart after genesis, the standalone node used 3-8% in five
of six samples (25% in one).

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/on_tick.go`: return early from `OnTick` when
`time < f.genesisTime`.
- `cl/phase1/forkchoice/on_tick_test.go`:
`TestOnTickBeforeGenesisIsNoop`.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestOnTickBeforeGenesisIsNoop` calls `OnTick(genesisTime -
1)` and requires it to return within 10 s with the store's time
unchanged. Before the change it failed at the 10 s timeout.
- `go test ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/... -count=1`
- `make lint`

subject: cl/beacon/handler: test the PTC aggregation order and skip it on a sync aggregate error (#24683)
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #24662, addressing the review points on its approval.

- Regression test for the aggregation order:
`TestProduceBeaconBodyIncludesPTCVotesReceivedDuringPayloadWait` puts a
PTC vote into `epbsPool.PayloadAttestations` from inside the mocked
`ForkChoiceUpdate`, so it arrives while the payload is being built, and
asserts the produced body carries it. The state gets its own config copy
with the Gloas fork epoch, so `GetPTC` works for the parent slot. With
the #24662 change reversed locally, the body has 0 attestations; with
it, 1.
- `syncAggregateErr` is checked right after `wg.Wait()`, before the PTC
aggregation, so a failed sync aggregate no longer pays for up to
`PtcSize` signature decompressions whose result is discarded. The
`executionErr` check stays after the aggregation because the Gloas
partial body is still used with an external bid.
- The nil guard on `aggregatePayloadAttestations`'s result is dropped:
it always returns a list.

## Testing

- `go test ./cl/beacon/handler/`
- `make lint` (twice)

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/network/services: verify gossip signatures with the message epoch's fork version (#24544)
body:
## Summary

Around a fork, Caplin verified gossip and pool signatures with the wrong
fork version and rejected valid messages.

- **Proposer preferences.** Preferences for the first Gloas epoch are
signed in the last Fulu epoch with
`compute_fork_version(proposal_epoch)`. Caplin took the domain from the
dependent state, which is still Fulu, and rejected every preference for
the fork epoch (`invalid proposer preferences signature`), from its own
VC and from gossip.
- **Other gossip messages.** Attestations, aggregates, sync committee
messages and contributions, and data column sidecar proposer signatures
took the domain from the head state's fork. When the first slot of a
fork has no block, the head state is still the old fork's, so
attestations, sync committee messages and contributions signed for the
new fork failed with `invalid bls signature` until the next block.
Aggregates of that slot are still ignored earlier, by the epoch range
check, until a block of the new epoch is seen; that check is unchanged.
The aggregate selection proof and aggregator signature always used the
head state's current fork version, so aggregates from the last epoch of
the old fork that arrived after the head crossed the fork were rejected;
they now verify. Data column sidecars of the first block of a new fork
are checked against the pre-fork head state, so they fail even when no
slot is skipped (the devnet below starts in Fulu, so it did not exercise
the sidecar fixes). With slot 64 skipped, each Caplin node rejected
about 130 valid messages from its own VC for that slot (128 sync
committee messages and the slot's attestations). The blob sidecar
proposer signature had a related bug: it took the fork of the parent
block's slot instead of the sidecar's.

The fix adds `fork.ComputeDomainAtEpoch`, which uses the fork version
the config schedules for an epoch, and calls it with each message's own
epoch. This matches what honest validators sign (the validator spec
signs with the head state processed through empty slots up to the duty)
and how Lighthouse verifies these messages (`fork_at_epoch`). It also
fixes two epoch arguments that were not epochs: the aggregate selection
proof used `slot * SLOTS_PER_EPOCH`, and the aggregator signature used
the state's slot.

Proposer and attester slashings are unchanged: they must stay valid when
included in a block, whose processing takes the fork from the state, and
they can carry evidence from older forks.

## Changes

- `cl/fork/fork.go`: `ComputeDomainAtEpoch`.
- `cl/phase1/network/services`: attestation, aggregate and proof, sync
committee message, sync contribution, blob sidecar, data column sidecar
and proposer preferences validation use the message epoch's fork
version.
- `cl/phase1/network/services` tests: removes
`TestVerifySyncCommitteeMessageSignatureUsesMessageSlotDomain` and
`TestVerifySyncContributionAggregatedSignatureUsesContributionSlotDomain`
(from #24489), which expected the domain from the state's fork field.
`TestGossipSignatureDomainsUseMessageEpochForkVersion` now preserves
their `"previous epoch"` regression case: the head is at the first slot
of the new fork and the message is from the previous fork’s last slot.
- `cl/beacon/handler/epbs_test.go`: the proposer preferences boundary
test signs with the spec domain.

## Testing

- **TDD:** each new test failed before the change:
`TestGossipSignatureDomainsUseMessageEpochForkVersion` (sync committee
messages, sync contributions and aggregates, at the first slot of the
new fork with the head still in the old fork, and at the last slot of
the old fork with the head already in the new one),
`TestAttestationSignatureDomainUsesTargetEpochForkVersion`,
`TestDataColumnSidecarProposerSignatureUsesHeaderEpochForkVersion`,
`TestBlobSidecarProposerSignatureUsesHeaderEpochForkVersion`,
`TestProposerPreferencesServiceSignatureDomainUsesProposalEpochForkVersion`.
- Devnet with slot 64 skipped: no `invalid bls signature` or `invalid
proposer preferences signature` on either Caplin node.
- `make lint`
- `make erigon integration`
- `go test ./cl/beacon/handler/... ./cl/fork/...
./cl/phase1/network/services/...`

## Devnet

Devnet used below: a local Kurtosis network with Lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0
(beacon node and VCs), Teku 26.9.1, Prysm v7.2.0 and two Caplin nodes on
v3.7.1 plus this change (one as a separate `caplin` service, one
embedded in Erigon), 128 validators per participant (Caplin 40%), Fulu
at genesis, Gloas at epoch 2, and spamoor sending transactions and
blobs. Fault runs also skipped the proposals of slots 64 and 65 and
restarted the embedded Erigon at slot 67. Every run used one image with
all the fixes in this series, so the runs show the combined effect, not
one PR in isolation.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/sentinel: keep peers through Status/Goodbye limits and failed handshakes (#24627)
body:
## Summary

Two fixes for peers that Caplin rejected or locked out although they had
not misbehaved.

**1. Status and Goodbye rate limits recover within a second.** The
inbound req/resp rate limiter keeps a token bucket per (peer, protocol).
Buckets and punishments are not cleared when a peer disconnects; a
bucket is dropped only after more than 10 minutes without use. Status
refilled at 0.33 tokens/s (burst 5) and Goodbye at 0.1 tokens/s (burst
1). An exhausted bucket punished the peer for 30 s, and during that time
every request on that protocol was answered with InvalidRequest without
being read.

A dialing peer sends Status on every new connection, and may send
Goodbye before it disconnects:

> The dialing client MUST send a `Status` request upon connection.

> Client MAY send goodbye messages upon disconnection.

A peer that reconnected every second or two ran out of Status tokens,
was locked out for 30 s, and its handshake Status was rejected. A
Goodbye sent within 10 s of the previous one was rejected, so its reason
was never read.

Status and Goodbye now refill at 1 token/s with bursts of 5 and 1, the
same limits Prysm v7.2.0 uses for these two protocols, and an over-limit
Status or Goodbye is rejected without the 30 s punishment, so the bucket
recovers within a second. Other protocols keep their limits and
punishment.

Goodbye was decoded with the loose decoder, which accepts a declared
length up to 16 MiB; `Ping.DecodeSSZ` then ignored anything after the
first 8 bytes, so longer payloads were accepted, and the decoder did not
check for data after the message, so trailing bytes were accepted too.
It now uses the exact decoder that Ping and Status already use: a
declared length other than 8 bytes is rejected before the payload is
read, and trailing bytes are rejected, both with InvalidRequest. A
Goodbye that fails to decode for another reason also gets InvalidRequest
instead of a stream reset (unless the stream itself was reset):

> If steps (1), (2), or (3) fail due to invalid, malformed, or
inconsistent data, the responder MUST respond in error.

The exact decoder reads to the end of the stream to detect trailing
bytes, so it relies on the requester closing its write side, which the
spec requires ("The requester MUST close the write side of the stream
once it finishes writing the request message").

**2. Failed handshakes stop our dials instead of banning the peer.**
Three status handshakes that failed with an error, with no more than 10
minutes between consecutive failures, put a peer into `bannedPeers`, the
same 30-minute cache used for peers banned for misbehaviour.
`handleNewConnection` then closed every connection that peer opened,
before any status exchange and without logging why.

A handshake can fail without the peer misbehaving, for example around a
restart, while the remote may still hold the connection from before. In
the devnet run below, the restarted node logged three failed handshakes
with Teku within about 3 s, starting one second after the restart. On
`main` that bans Teku for 30 minutes, including the connections Teku
opens itself.

Handshake failures now work in two steps:
- The 3rd failure makes the peer undialable for 30 minutes, and every
further failure renews the mark while the failure count is live (until
10 minutes after the last failure). The new `Pool.Dialable` is false for
banned and undialable peers and for peers whose connections are refused.
Sentinel installs it as the dial policy of the libp2p connection gater
(`Gater.InterceptPeerDial`), so we don't open a new connection to such a
peer, whether the dial comes from our dial paths, a req/resp request
(the status handshake uses the same handler) or GossipSub. libp2p
consults this check only when there is no usable connection to the peer,
so it does not affect inbound connections or streams over an existing
connection. `ConnectWithPeer` also checks `Dialable` before calling
libp2p and returns "peer is not dialable", and the subnet peer search
skips such peers.
- Connections the peer opens are not refused for these failures and are
handshaked as usual (the peer limit still applies). The 10th failure
closes the peer, and its connections are refused until 10 minutes after
the last failure (the failure count's TTL is refreshed on every
failure).

A successful handshake clears the failure count and the undialable mark.
Peers banned through `BanPeer` are refused as before.

The third commit adds logging and two small fixes. Closing a connection
from a refused peer was not logged, handshake failures were logged only
at Trace, and `BanPeer` logged neither a ban nor a skipped ban. There
are now Debug logs, with the peer ID, when a connection from a refused
peer is closed (with direction and address), when a handshake fails
(with the failure count), when a peer becomes undialable, when repeated
failures make us refuse it, when `BanPeer` bans a peer or skips the ban
because there are fewer than `gracePeerCount` active peers, and when a
Goodbye is received (with its reason code).
- A failed handshake's error contained the raw response body, which is
the length-prefixed snappy stream rather than the message. It is now
decoded with the existing `ResponseCode.ErrorMessage`, which caps the
message at 256 bytes. When the HTTP handler fails before there is a
response code (for example, the stream to the peer could not be opened),
its plain-text message is kept, also capped at 256 bytes.
- The Goodbye handler passed the key and the peer ID to
`Peerstore().Get` in the wrong order, so the agent version lookup failed
and its Warn for reason codes above 250 did not fire.

Known limit of the logging: `ErrorMessage` returns an empty message for
InvalidRequest (code 1), as on `main` (`service.go` relies on that), so
a handshake rejected with InvalidRequest is logged with the code only.

Devnet (Kurtosis; Fulu at genesis, Gloas at epoch 2, 12 s slots;
Lighthouse v8.3.0-rc.0, Teku 26.9.1, Prysm v7.2.0, Nimbus v26.10.0 and
two Caplin nodes; one Caplin node restarted at slot 67). These runs were
made before the review changes (dial policy in the connection gater,
undialable mark renewed on later failures):
- Without these changes:
- One Caplin node rate-limited three Status requests from Nimbus sent
about 1.4 s apart, and each Caplin node rate-limited three Goodbye
messages that Prysm sent during repeated bad-peer disconnection
attempts.
- The part of Teku's log that was kept (from slot 83) shows Teku
connecting to the restarted Caplin node 8 times between slots 89 and
171; each time the connection closed within about 10 ms and Teku logged
`Failed to send status ... PeerDisconnectedException`.
- With these changes, in a run that also included #24512, #24544-#24548,
#24550 and the chain tip polling fix:
- Neither Caplin node logged a rate-limited request. That run did not
have the Prysm disconnection loop or the Nimbus reconnects seen above,
so for (1) it shows no regression rather than the fix itself.
- The restarted node logged three failed handshakes with Teku within
about 3 s and `Peer became undialable`; Teku connected to it at slot 76
and stayed connected to the end of the run. At slot 100 every CL node
had 5 peers.

Not changed here:
- A rate-limited request is still answered with InvalidRequest and the
stream is closed. The spec asks the responder to delay instead:
> The responder MAY rate-limit chunks by withholding each chunk until
capacity is available. The responder MUST NOT respond with an error or
close the stream when rate limiting.
- Rate limits and punishment for the other protocols.
- `BanPeer` still does not ban or disconnect while fewer than
`gracePeerCount` (32) peers are active; it now only logs the skipped
ban.

## Changes

- `cl/sentinel/handlers/rate_limiter.go`: Status and Goodbye refill at 1
token/s (burst 5 and 1); new `noPunishment` flag on
`protocolRateConfig`, set for these two, so an exhausted bucket only
rejects the request.
- `cl/sentinel/handlers/heartbeats.go`: decode Goodbye with
`DecodeAndReadNoForkDigestExact` and answer a malformed one with
InvalidRequest; Goodbye Debug log and `Peerstore().Get` argument order.
- `cl/sentinel/peers/peers_pool.go`: `undialable` cache, `Dialable`,
`RefuseConnections`; `RecordHandshakeFailure` returns the count and
whether the count has just reached the undialable threshold, and renews
the undialable mark on every failure from the 3rd while the count is
live; `RecordHandshakeSuccess` (in place of the empty `AddPeer`, which
main has removed) clears both; `handshakeFailures` holds 100,000
entries, like the other two caches.
- `cl/sentinel/discovery.go`: dial paths check `Dialable`
(`ConnectWithPeer` reports a refused dial as "peer is not dialable", the
subnet peer search skips the peer); `handleNewConnection` calls
`RecordHandshakeSuccess` after a successful handshake, refuses
connections per `RefuseConnections` (before the handshake, and after the
failure that reaches the limit) and takes the connection's direction and
address for logging.
- `cl/p2p/gater.go`, `cl/p2p/p2p.go`, `cl/p2p/p2p_interface.go`,
`cl/sentinel/sentinel.go`: `Gater.SetDialPolicy`, exposed as
`P2PManager.SetDialPolicy`; `InterceptPeerDial` refuses a dial that the
policy rejects; Sentinel installs `Pool.Dialable` as the policy.
- `cl/sentinel/handshake/handshake.go`: decode the error message of a
failed handshake, or keep the handler's plain-text message when there is
no response code, capped at 256 bytes.
- `cl/sentinel/service/service.go`: `BanPeer` logs a ban or a skipped
ban, and reads the peer ID with `GetPid()`.

## Testing

- **TDD:** these failed before their changes:
`TestRateLimiter_StatusRecoversWithoutPunishment` (Status v1 and v2),
`TestRateLimiter_GoodbyeRecoversWithoutPunishment`,
`TestGoodbyeRejectsOversizedRequest`, `TestGoodbyeRejectsTrailingBytes`,
`TestGoodbyeRejectsMaxDeclaredLength`,
`TestHandshakeFailuresDoNotRefuseThePeersLaterConnection`,
`TestHandshakeFailuresRefuseConnectionsAtLimit`,
`TestHandshakeFailureThresholds`,
`TestHandshakeFailureRenewsUndialableMark`,
`TestRecordHandshakeSuccessClearsHandshakeFailuresAndUndialableStatus`,
`TestGaterDialPolicy`, `TestNewInstallsDialPolicy`,
`TestValidatePeerDecodesAndCapsErrorMessage`,
`TestValidatePeerReportsCappedHandlerError` and
`TestGoodbyeLogsAgentVersionForHighReason`.
`TestOnConnectionLogsActualTransport` now also checks the refusal log
line. `TestRepeatedHandshakeFailuresStopOutboundDials` is a guard for
behaviour that is unchanged: no redial after three failures.
`TestGaterDialPolicy` also checks that the gater accepts the rejected
peer's inbound connection and that a stream over that connection still
works.
- `TestGoodbye` now half-closes its stream before reading the response,
as the exact decoder requires. The Ping and Goodbye tests share one
stream helper.
- `make lint`
- `go build ./...`
- `make erigon integration`
- `go test ./cl/p2p/... ./cl/sentinel/... ./cl/phase1/network/gossip/`
- `go test -race -count=3 -run
'Gater|Dial|Handshake|RecordHandshake|Goodbye' ./cl/p2p/ ./cl/sentinel/
./cl/sentinel/peers/ ./cl/sentinel/handlers/`
- `go test ./cl/sentinel/handlers/ -run
'Goodbye|Ping|Status|RateLimiter' -race -count=3`

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/stages: recover the served head and FULL payloads after a restart (#24548)
body:
## Summary

Two problems kept an Erigon node with embedded Caplin from rejoining
after a restart around the Gloas fork. One commit each, plus follow-up
commits.

1. **The served head stayed on the anchor.** The beacon API serves
attestation data from the synced head state, which, after a non-stale
ForwardSync, only the ForkChoice stage updated (apart from blocks this
node publishes through the beacon API). After ForwardSync, and after a
ChainTipSync timeout while the node had peers, the stage graph went
straight to ChainTipSync while the node was below the current slot, so
the imported head was not published until a block for the current slot
arrived. A node restarted before finality forward-synced from genesis to
slot 65 in eight seconds, then served the genesis root for about seven
minutes while ChainTipSync timed out every 25 seconds; Lighthouse banned
it less than half a second after its first attestation. Now, when a
non-stale ForwardSync or a ChainTipSync would otherwise go to
ChainTipSync while the node is below the current slot, it goes to
ForkChoice first if the fork choice head differs from the served head; a
ForwardSync that is still epochs behind continues with ForwardSync. For
ForwardSync this also holds without peers (a failed peer count counts as
zero peers); ChainTipSync without peers already went to ForkChoice. At
the current slot ForwardSync still goes to ChainTipSync, which does not
wait for blocks there. ForkChoice never goes straight back to
ForkChoice, so a head that fails to publish cannot stop block fetching.
ForwardSync now flushes its blocks to an embedded EL before it returns
normally, so that hop no longer fails with `block not found` unless the
flush fails or keeps rows back after a gap (the flush is best effort, as
in ChainTipSync). ForkChoice still runs before ChainTipSync has
re-verified stored envelopes, so until the next ChainTipSync cycle it
can publish a head that misses FULL payloads; such a head is still
recent, unlike the anchor.
2. **FULL payload status was lost across the restart.** Payload
verification state is kept in memory, and with an embedded EL
ForwardSync replays stored envelopes without validating them, so after a
restart they have no status. Fork choice then exposes only the EMPTY
variant of such a block, and children built on its FULL payload are
imported but unreachable. The bounded sweep that re-verifies stored
envelopes ran only when ChainTipSync started at or past the target slot,
but a node normally enters it one slot behind. A node restarted three
slots after the fork kept building on the EMPTY slot 66 for about 60
slots (`wrong head block` from the EL on every build, PTC attestations
rejected) and recovered only when justification moved past it. The sweep
now also runs when ChainTipSync starts below the target slot in Gloas,
after the execution engine reports ready and before ChainTipSync waits
for blocks, so it runs on every ChainTipSync cycle in which an attached
execution engine is ready. A `NewPayload` that returns no status after
the sweep's time budget has expired is not recorded as a verdict. When
the head moves to a child of the head the sweep saw last, the sweep
checks the new head in the same cycle, so after a restart it repairs one
stored payload per cycle instead of one every two cycles. At the target
slot it still runs after the wait for the head's envelope, so an
envelope that arrives there and fails its first `NewPayload` is retried
in the same cycle.

Not changed here:
- While ForwardSync runs, attestation data still comes from the anchor
head (in the devnet up to two minutes). The pool change in the separate
PR #24547 keeps the node from publishing the resulting attestations;
reporting the node as syncing in that window is left for a follow-up.
- After ForwardSync the published head can still be up to about two
epochs behind, since ForwardSync hands over to ChainTipSync once the
node is within an epoch of the target.
- While the head does not move, the re-verification sweep processes the
unverified envelopes it collects from the head back oldest-first under
one shared two-second budget, and keeps its cursor unless every item
ran. If the EL keeps timing out on the oldest one, every cycle can spend
the budget on it, and newer payloads, including the head's, stay
unverified. An envelope that cannot be read from disk is skipped without
stopping the batch, so the cursor can move past it. Both already happen
on `main`; this PR does not change them and makes the sweep run more
often. Left for a follow-up.
- A stale ForwardSync still goes straight to ChainTipSync after
publishing the head itself, and that publication gives up silently if
the head state is not available.
- `headUnpublished` compares block roots only. If the sweep makes the
FULL variant of the served head available without changing the root, it
is published only when ForkChoice next runs for another reason.
- Payload verification state is still lost on a restart. With an
embedded EL, ForwardSync does not validate the envelopes it replays, so
every stored payload of the unfinalized range is re-verified after a
restart, at about one block per ChainTipSync cycle while those blocks
sit above the head. Keeping the status across the replay is left for a
follow-up.

## Changes

- `cl/phase1/stages/clstages.go`: `Args.headUnpublished`,
`catchUpAfterImport` for ForwardSync and ChainTipSync, and a ForwardSync
fallback to ForkChoice without peers when the head is unpublished and
the node is below the current slot.
- `cl/phase1/stages/chain_tip_sync.go`: also run
`verifyUnverifiedGloasPayloads` below the target slot in Gloas, once the
execution engine is ready; in the sweep, do not record a `NewPayload`
that ran out of time, and check the new head whenever the walk does not
start at it.
- `cl/phase1/stages/forward_sync.go`: flush the block collector before a
normal return when the execution client supports insertion.

## Testing

- **TDD:** `TestChainTipSyncVerifiesStoredGloasPayloadWhileBehind` fails
on `main`. The rows of
`TestCatchUpPublishesForkChoiceHeadBeforeChainTipSync` that expect
ForkChoice failed with the transition changes reverted (the test needs
the new `headUnpublished` field).
`TestChainTipSyncReverifiesHeadEnvelopeReceivedAtTarget` failed (one
`NewPayload` call instead of two) while the sweep ran before the
at-target envelope wait. The `forward sync, no peers, head unpublished`
case of the first test failed (ChainTipSync instead of ForkChoice)
before the zero-peer follow-up commit.
`TestChainTipSyncDoesNotVerifyStoredGloasPayloadWhileExecutionEngineIsBusy`
failed (one `NewPayload` call instead of none) while the sweep ran
before the wait for the execution engine.
