The `/eth/v1/events` handler writes to the socket on the same goroutine
that drains its subscription channel (capacity 128). The emitters use
the blocking `feed.Send`, which waits for every subscriber, and the
beacon API write timeout defaults to a year. So one SSE client that
stops reading fills the channel and then blocks `SendAttestation`
(called from the batch signature verifier), `SendBlock` (block import)
and `SendChainReorg` for as long as the connection stays open.

Writes now go through a per-connection writer goroutine with a queue
limited to 1024 messages and 64 MiB. The handler only enqueues; if
either limit is exceeded the stream is closed and both subscriptions are
dropped, so emitters never wait on a client's socket. The writer stops
at the next message boundary and the in-flight write is aborted with a
past write deadline, so a slow client that keeps reading is cut
immediately instead of being drained. `Send` keeps its blocking
semantics for everything else
(`TestFinalizedCheckpointEmittedOutsideLock` still relies on that).

The writer arms a 30s write deadline before each write and clears it
after the flush, and stops on the first error. Without that, the
teardown after an overflow would wait on a write stuck on the stalled
socket until the server `WriteTimeout` (one year by default).

Behaviour change: a client that falls behind is now dropped; before, it
was never dropped. The teardown aborts the in-flight write, so the
chunked response ends without the terminating chunk: the client gets
`unexpected EOF` and the last event can be cut in the middle, which a
compliant SSE parser drops. 1024 messages and 64 MiB are budgets, not
tuned values: the byte limit keeps a few slow clients from holding
gigabytes of encoded `data_column_sidecar`/`blob_sidecar` events, and
still fits a full per-block burst of column sidecars. For high-rate
topics the queue, not the 30s deadline, decides when a client is dropped
(a full stall overflows 1024 messages above roughly 34 events/s).

The 30s per-write deadline replaces `--beacon.api.write.timeout`
(`a.routerCfg.WriteTimeout`, the value `router.go` passes to
`http.Server.WriteTimeout`) for this endpoint, so a configured value
below 30s no longer applies to the event stream.

Testing:

```
go test -count=3 -run 'TestEventStream|TestWriteEventStream' ./cl/beacon/handler/
go test -race -run 'TestEventStream|TestFinalizedCheckpointEmittedOutsideLock' ./cl/beacon/handler/ ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/
go test -short ./cl/beacon/...
```

Without the change `TestEventStreamSlowClientDoesNotBlockEmitters` fails
with "a stalled event stream client blocked the event emitter", and
without the write deadline `TestEventStreamOverflowClosesStalledStream`
fails because the handler never returns.

Closes #24526.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/forkchoice: check header presence instead of loading a state for pending envelopes (#25098)
body:
Part of #25120.

## Problem

`validatePendingEnvelopeCommitments`
(`cl/phase1/forkchoice/on_execution_payload.go`) calls
`forkGraph.GetState(root, false)` under `f.mu.RLock` only to test that
the block's state exists. When the root is not the fork graph's current
state, this reads a dumped state from disk and replays blocks while the
fork-choice lock is held. The state is then thrown away: the envelope
apply that follows loads the state again by itself.

## What changed

`validatePendingEnvelopeCommitments` checks header presence
(`forkGraph.GetHeader(root)`) instead of loading the state. The block is
stored before the transition runs and the header is published only after
the transition succeeds, so header presence (not `GetBlock`) is the
marker of a validated post-state. The `GetBlock` check and the rest of
the function are unchanged.

Effects:
- The work under `f.mu.RLock` drops from a possible disk read plus block
replay to two map lookups.
- When the header exists (the normal case), each pending-envelope retry
now loads the state once (in the apply) instead of twice. In the rare
case where `AddChainSegment` stored the block and its state but failed
before it published the header, the apply still loads the state twice,
as before, but now both loads run under the write lock.
- When a header exists but its state cannot be loaded, the envelope's
commitments are now checked before the apply. These checks use only the
block and the envelope, so an envelope with invalid commitments is now
rejected at this point instead of waiting in the queue until it ages
out.

No interface changed and no new constants were added.

## Testing

TDD. `TestValidatePendingEnvelopeCommitmentsUsesHeaderAsReadinessMarker`
fails on the base production code for the intended reason and passes
with the change: a stored block without a header is not ready, a block
with a header is ready, and neither case loads a state (a fake fork
graph counts `GetState` calls). The existing pending-envelope test fakes
got a `GetHeader` method.

Commands: `go test ./cl/phase1/stages/ ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/...
-count=1`, `go test -race ./cl/phase1/forkchoice/`, `go build ./...` and
`make lint` (clean on repeated runs) all pass.

## Not included

- Head event state root: an earlier version of this PR also took the
head event's state root from the fork-choice header instead of calling
`headState.HashSSZ()` in `emitHeadEvent`. Review showed that this does
not remove the cold hash. That hash also fills the Merkle caches of the
head state that is then copied into synced data. Without it, the next
block import on that head hashes the cold copy in full while it holds
the fork-choice write lock. That change was dropped; a later change that
reuses warm states can handle it.
- Reusing warm head and previous-head states for `alwaysCopy` loads,
moving state loads out of `f.mu`, and parallel hashing are separate
follow-ups.

## Backport

Not planned for release/3.8. This is a small improvement: it removes one
unneeded state load per pending-envelope check. It does not fix a
correctness problem.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/transition/impl/eth2/statechange: avoid contended and no-op dirty marks in epoch processing (#25144)
body:
Part of #25136 (direction 1).

## Problem

On Hoodi (~1.14M active validators), the first block of each epoch runs
`ProcessEpoch` and the following state-root hash under the fork-choice
write lock. On our test node this takes about 0.85 s per epoch. More
than half of it comes from two implementation inefficiencies, not from
the spec work:

- **Rewards and penalties.** The parallel loop writes each balance
directly. Every write goes through `MarkLeafAsDirty`, which takes the
balances Merkle tree `RWMutex` read lock. Readers do not block each
other, but they all update the same reader count, so most of the step's
CPU is contention on that counter. This applies when the balances tree
exists, which is the normal case for a warm Fulu state.
- **Effective balance updates.** The effective balance is written
whenever the hysteresis condition is true, also when the new value
equals the old one. Validators at the maximum with excess balance meet
the condition in every epoch. On the Hoodi state, 120,912 validator
leaves become dirty but only 9 effective balances change, and the next
`HashSSZ` rehashes all of them.

## What changed

- The reward/penalty deltas are computed in parallel into a slice and
applied serially in eligible-index order. The delta computation does not
read balances and the eligible indices are unique, so the result is the
same.
- `ProcessEffectiveBalanceUpdates` skips the write when the new
effective balance equals the current one.

The post-epoch state bytes and root do not change.

Behaviour changes in callbacks, with no production consumer:
- `OnNewValidatorEffectiveBalance` no longer fires for no-op writes.
- `OnNewValidatorBalance` fires serially in eligible-index order instead
of concurrently.
- A compute error now leaves no balance written.

The antiquary installs neither hook (`state_antiquary.go`); it derives
historical balances and effective balances from the raw state bytes, so
state snapshots are not affected.

## Measurements

Real Hoodi state (~1.14M active validators, 1.67M registry), Apple M3
Pro, warm hashed state as on block import, base and this change run
interleaved, medians:

| | Base | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| **Fulu** rewards and penalties | ~115 ms (~1.3 s CPU) | ~17 ms (~53 ms
CPU) |
| **Fulu** `ProcessSlots` across the boundary | ~193 ms | ~87 ms |
| **Fulu** post-epoch `HashSSZ` | ~101 ms | ~20 ms |
| **Gloas** rewards and penalties (no balances tree) | ~27 ms | ~14 ms |
| **Gloas** `ProcessSlots` across the boundary | ~316 ms | ~305 ms |
| **Gloas** post-epoch `HashSSZ` | ~102 ms | ~23 ms |

A Gloas state upgraded from a hashed Fulu state keeps the balances tree;
there the rewards step goes from ~130 ms to ~17 ms. On Gloas the
boundary is dominated by the PTC window (~216 ms), which is handled
separately in #25143. The post-epoch root was identical between base and
this change on both forks.

`BenchmarkEpochProcessing` (synthetic, 200k validators, Fulu):
- RewardsAndPenalties: ~19 ms → ~3.3 ms
- EffectiveBalanceUpdatesAndHashSSZ: ~60 ms → ~1.3 ms

## Testing

TDD. These tests fail on the base for the intended reason and pass with
the change:
- only changed effective balances are written (Deneb, Fulu, Gloas; Deneb
covers the pre-Electra maximum);
- balance writes are serial and in eligible-index order;
- a compute error writes no balance.

`TestProcessEpochWarmRootMatchesColdRoot` runs a full `ProcessEpoch` on
Fulu and Gloas and checks that the warm post-epoch root equals the root
of the re-decoded state. It guards the dirty-mark changes and also
passes on the base. Output equivalence is covered by the existing
golden-state tests and the consensus spec tests.

- `go test -race` on `cl/transition/...`, `cl/phase1/core/state/...`,
`cl/merkle_tree/...` passes.
- `go test ./cl/phase1/... ./cl/transition/...` and `go build ./...`
pass.
- `make lint` (clean on repeated runs) and `make erigon integration`
pass.
- epoch_processing and sanity spec tests: the failing set is identical
to the merge base (outdated local Gloas fixtures and `mainnet_config`);
the pinned fixtures run in CI.

## Not included

- The other directions in #25136 (`attestation_data` without a full
state advance, gossip validation of the boundary block, precomputing the
next-epoch state).
- Rewards are still applied as one net delta per validator; this is the
same as before.

## Backport

Not planned for release/3.8. This is a performance improvement; it does
not fix a correctness problem.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/cltypes/solid, cl/phase1/core/state/raw: cache Gloas balances and inactivity scores roots incrementally (#25102)
body:
Part of #25120.

## Problem

From Gloas on, `raw.BeaconState` hashes `balances` and
`inactivity_scores` as progressive lists (EIP-7916). The Gloas branches
of `computeDirtyLeaves` called
`merkle_tree.ProgressiveBasicListRoot(list.Bytes(), ...)`, which
re-merkleizes the whole list on every hash. There was no cache like the
binary `MerkleTree` that Fulu uses.

Measured on the Hoodi node (about 1.14M validators): on a warm state,
changing 600 balances and hashing costs 41 ms in Gloas and 3.7 ms in
Fulu. Inactivity scores have the same cost. Balances change in every
block, so every block import (`VerifyTransition`, under the fork-choice
write lock) pays this, and so do many state copies and validations.
Hoodi upgrades to Gloas on 2026-10-26.

## What changed

- `cl/cltypes/solid/uint64slice_byte.go`: `byteBasedUint64Slice` gets a
progressive tree cache (`progressiveTrees`), built the same way as
`ValidatorSet.progressiveTrees`: one `merkle_tree.MerkleTree` per
progressive segment (capacities 1, 4, 16, ... chunks). Leaves are packed
32-byte chunks (4 values per leaf), and the length mix-in uses the
element count. `Set` and `Append` mark only the touched chunk as dirty;
a new leaf starts when `l%4 == 0`. `Pop`, `Clear` and `DecodeSSZ` drop
the cache. `CopyTo` deep-copies the trees, binds the leaf functions to
the destination buffer, and reuses the destination's tree storage when
it has some.
- `cl/cltypes/solid/uint64_list.go`: `uint64ListSSZ` forwards the new
`HashSSZProgressive` and `SetProgressiveHashing`.
- `cl/phase1/core/state/raw/hashing.go`: the Gloas branches for balances
and inactivity scores use the cached root. Other `Uint64ListSSZ`
implementations (which `SetBalances` / `SetInactivityScoresRaw` accept)
still use `ProgressiveBasicListRoot`.
- `cl/phase1/core/state/raw/setters.go`: `SetVersion` switches the cache
mode of both lists when crossing the Gloas boundary, like it already
does for validators, so the binary tree is released and not kept next to
the progressive one.

Pre-Gloas hashing is not changed. `cl/merkle_tree` is not changed. No
locking was added: the lists keep the same caller-serialized contract as
the existing binary tree and validator set caches.

## How it was tested

TDD. The new list tests did not compile on the base commit (the API was
missing). `origin/main` cost is the `gloas_uncached` benchmark below.

New tests:
- `cl/cltypes/solid/uint64_list_progressive_test.go`: root equals
`ProgressiveBasicListRoot` for lengths around chunk and segment
boundaries (0, 1, 4, 5, 20, 21, 84, 85); after `Set`; after an append
inside a chunk, across a chunk and across a segment; after `Clear` then
`Append`; after `Pop` and `DecodeSSZ` (including empty); a randomized
test mixing `Set`/`Append`/`Pop`/`DecodeSSZ`; copy independence (copy,
then mutate source and destination differently); copy between lists with
different backing buffer sizes; copy from a cold source clears a stale
destination cache; destination tree reuse; cache-mode switch; and
`TestUint64ListWarmProgressiveHashIsIncremental`, which checks that 600
changes on a warm 1.14M list recompute at most 1,200 leaves instead of
the whole list.
- `cl/phase1/core/state/raw/hashing_gloas_test.go`: `SetVersion`
switches both lists in and out of progressive mode and Gloas hashing
uses the list's cache; a fallback test for non-list implementations;
`TestSetVersionAcrossGloasInvalidatesRoots` now has non-empty lists.
- `cl/phase1/core/state/upgrade_test.go`:
`TestUpgradeToGloasStateRootMatchesDecodedState`: a Fulu state with warm
caches upgraded with `UpgradeToGloas` hashes to the same root as the
same state decoded fresh.

Commands:
- `go test -race ./cl/cltypes/solid/ ./cl/merkle_tree/ -count=1`: pass.
- `go test ./cl/phase1/core/state/... ./cl/transition/... -count=1`:
pass.
- `go build ./...` and `make lint` (clean twice): pass.
- Spec tests: the local consensus-spec fixture cache is older than the
v1.7.0-beta.4 fixtures that `test-fixtures.json` pins, so many Gloas
cases fail on the base commit too. I ran `go test -tags=spectest
-run='Test/mainnet/gloas/' -v` in `cl/spectest` on the base commit and
on this branch: the same 1,483 cases ran with identical pass/fail
results (322 pass, 1,161 fail). For all five
`gloas/ssz_static/BeaconState` cases, both builds compute the same state
roots. `fulu` and `electra` `ssz_static/BeaconState`, `sanity` and
`epoch_processing` pass (543 cases); only `mainnet_config` fails,
because of the same fixture drift. CI with the pinned fixtures still has
to confirm the Gloas spec tests.

Benchmarks (`cl/cltypes/solid/uint64_list_bench_test.go`, Apple M3 Pro,
1.14M-element list, 600 random `Set`s then hash, `-benchtime=20x
-count=3`):

| Case | Time | Allocated |
|---|---:|---:|
| Fulu, binary cache (`HashSSZ`) | 0.99-1.00 ms | 0 B |
| Gloas, new progressive cache | 1.00 ms | 0 B |
| Gloas, origin/main (`ProgressiveBasicListRoot`) | 16.8-22.4 ms | 18.2
MB |
| `CopyTo` a warm list into a new list | 1.0-1.2 ms | 24.6 MB |
| `CopyTo` a warm list into a reused list | 0.6-1.0 ms | 320 B |

So the warm Gloas hash now costs the same as Fulu. The progressive cache
holds 14.9 MB per 1.14M-element list (measured with `runtime.MemStats`
after GC), so about 29.7 MB per state for both lists. In Gloas this
replaces the binary cache, which is released on the fork switch. The
fresh-copy allocation includes the 9.1 MB value buffer.

## Not included

- Validator tree parallelism, participation lists, fork-graph /
state-loading / lock changes, and persisting caches (other PRs).
- Two pre-existing bugs in `byteBasedUint64Slice`, left for a follow-up:
`UnmarshalJSON` sets the length before it appends, so the list doubles
in length; and the binary `MerkleTree` path does not add a leaf when
appending after `Clear` or after decoding an empty list, because it
detects new chunks by buffer growth (both panic with index out of range
on the base commit).

## Backport
Not planned for release/3.8 for now. Without it, a Gloas block costs
about 41 ms more hashing on the measured node; that is slower, not
wrong. We will decide after watching Hoodi run Gloas (from 2026-10-26)
on release/3.8.

author: Andrew Ashikhmin
subject: cl, execution: complete payload preparation coverage and hardening (#24939)
body:
Closes #23419.

Complete the remaining payload preparation hardening, and prove that
normal block production collects the prepared execution build only when
its payload ID matches. Missing, failed, skipped and mismatched
preparation keep the normal collection window.

## Changes

**Real-module coverage**
- 22 handler-to-execution-module cases: ordinary pre-Gloas slots,
pre-Fulu epoch boundaries, the first Gloas slot and EMPTY cover
prepared, absent, failed and mismatched preparation. FULL and
FULL-to-EMPTY cover intentional preparation skips, absent records and
mismatched records.
- Each case checks the collected ID, the execution parent, collection
timing, and that preparation leaves the source state's slot unchanged.
- The matrix uses a shared fixture and a case table. It runs in the full
suite behind the canonical `testing.Short()` guard.
- Naming changes, the metric refactor and documentation edits skip TDD
because they do not change behavior; existing tests and documentation
checks cover them.

**Import coordination**
- Builder startup is coordinated with canonical imports by slot. An
import that starts cancels a running speculative startup. Preparation is
refused while an import in its slot range is registered.
- Import registrations:
  - block imports (`onBlock`, `processAndStoreBlock`);
- envelope imports, registered after the builder signature check and
keyed by the known block slot;
  - envelope consensus validation;
  - the stage `NewPayloadWithAdmission` path.
- Queued gossip blocks hold no import claim before the expected proposer
is checked:
- A gossip block parked before its proposer is verified holds no claim.
Unknown parents leave the job queued without taking validation capacity
or accessing state. Parents at the same or a later slot cause terminal
rejection before state access. The retry checks the expected proposer
before starting an import. Missing parent state leaves the job queued
without cancelling preparation; a wrong proposer removes the job. A
block with the expected proposer retains its claim if processing returns
a dependency or back-off error.
- Blocks parked after full gossip validation (data availability, parent
envelope pending, too early, back-off) and locally published blocks keep
their claim between retries until the job is removed or expires.
- Envelopes queued in the gossip service because their block is unknown
register their root until the job is removed or expires. They refuse
preparation only once that root is a known block in range, and the
registration never cancels a running attempt. Envelopes queued on
admission-busy are not registered: the in-flight envelope for the same
block and builder claims after authentication, and so does the queued
one when it is processed.
- Envelopes parked in fork choice count only for blocks after the
selected head. The selected head's own parked envelope may never import
(for example, withheld data columns), so preparation still primes its
EMPTY fallback, as before. Persisted envelopes (index-repair markers)
never count.

**Builder ID, metrics and flag**
- Deadline expiry alone does not discard a successful builder startup
result. Import interruption is tracked independently of context
cancellation and prevents recording the attempt as prepared even if the
deadline fired first. A changed selected head also prevents recording it
as prepared.
- `caplin_payload_preparation_outcomes_total{outcome}` uses a fixed set
of reasons. New labels:
  - `too_early`;
  - `busy` when the wait is caused by block processing;
- the cancellation cause from admission (`busy` for an import, `late`
for the deadline).
- The PTC wait counts `pending` once.
-
`caplin_payload_preparation_collections_total{outcome="reused|absent|mismatch"}`
reports whether collection reused a matching prepared payload. `absent`
also covers disabled or unsupported preparation.
- `--caplin.payload-preparation.disable` covers embedded and standalone
Caplin and disables preparation without disabling the validator API or
normal block production. Preparation is enabled by default when the
validator API is enabled and the execution client supports direct
payload building. The flag path logs once.

**Builder reuse, cache and payload IDs**
- An exact live execution builder is reused after an A → B → A head
flip, with the existing bounded eviction.
- Decoded FULL-parent execution requests are cached for up to eight
roots. The LRU is built in the constructor, and concurrent misses are
coalesced, so a root is decoded at most once while it is retained.
- Deterministic slot-transition and withdrawal derivation failures are
memoized for the whole preparation key. Cancellation, contention,
storage and EL failures stay retryable.
- Engine API payload-ID decoding is shared with the hybrid client:
big-endian, and exactly eight bytes. The direct client's wire format is
unchanged.

## Known limitations

- FULL and FULL-to-EMPTY are intentional preparation skips with
successful normal FCU and collection coverage. FULL priming is tracked
in #23551. #24938 lands after this PR and flips those matrix cases.
- After the PTC deadline, an attempt refused because an import is in
progress waits for the next quarter-slot tick. This is the bounded
post-PTC retry of #24119 item 2.
- The import claim ends when fork choice has processed the block, before
the stage publishes the new head. A late block can therefore let
preparation build briefly on the old head. This heals on the next tick.
- `onBlock` registers its import on entry, before validation, so a block
that turns out invalid can cancel a running attempt for the length of
that call.
- A gossip-verified block parked on data availability or a missing
parent envelope (`ErrParentEnvelopePending`) can hold its claim until
the 30 s job expiry. Withheld columns, or a parent envelope available to
the next proposer but not to us, can suppress our preparation for the
next slot or two.
- While a claim covers the range, each tick repeats the state copy
before admission is refused.
- An unauthenticated envelope queued for a block that is not yet known
refuses preparation for one queue pass after that block becomes known.
- After an A → B → A builder reuse, the collections metric can report
`mismatch` although production reused a warm builder.

---------

Co-authored-by: kewei <kewei.train@gmail.com>

author: Kewei
subject: cl, cmd: make beacon state copies cheap and keep the fork graph's current state inside fork choice (#25151)
body:
Fixes #25111.

## Problem

Block import mutates the fork graph's current state in place under the
fork-choice write lock. `GetStateAtBlockRoot(root, false)` handed the
same object to callers that hashed and copied it after the lock was
released, and some current-state copies (checkpoint states, the
operation pruner, Beacon API collection getters) were taken without the
lock. `raw.CopyInto` and the Merkle branch methods also did not take the
raw state mutex.

Reproduced on main (details in #25111): torn copies with stale Merkle
caches (wrong state roots in the synced head, head event and attestation
data), and a reader's `HashSSZ` that corrupted the fork graph's state,
so a valid block was rejected, stored in `badBlocks`, and `currentState`
was cleared.

## What changed

Two commits; reviewing them one by one is easier. The full reasoning,
the registry-mutation audit and the test list are in the commit
messages.

**Commit 1: make beacon state copies cheap.** Private copies under the
read lock are only acceptable if a copy is cheap, so this comes first.
It does not change any locking.
- The pubkey index is an immutable base map with full 48-byte keys,
shared by a state and its copies, plus a small per-state delta. A copy
no longer rebuilds the map. Full keys remove the 64-bit hash collision
risk of the old map. The base is still built eagerly where it was built
before (New, InitBeaconState, decode).
- Registry setters keep the index correct; this also fixes the
historical states reader, which left the index empty.
- Gloas `ValidatorSet.CopyTo` reuses the destination progressive trees,
`ParticipationBitList.CopyTo` copies in bulk, and `ptcWindow` is
deep-copied (it was shared and raced on the first hash).
- Copy into a reused spare, 1.14M validators: Fulu ~81 ms → ~11.7 ms,
Gloas ~80 ms / 70.9 MB → ~11.1 ms / 9.3 MB.

**Commit 2: keep the fork graph's current state inside fork choice.** No
pointer to the current state object leaves fork choice anymore.
- `ForkGraph.GetState(root, alwaysCopy)` is replaced by
`CurrentStateLocked` (valid only under `f.mu`) and `ReplayState` (a
private state from disk).
- `ForkChoiceStore.GetStateAtBlockRoot(root)` always returns a private
state: the current state is copied under `f.mu.RLock`, other roots are
replayed without `f.mu`. Callers that already hold `f.mu` use locked
variants that do not lock again.
- Checkpoint-state builds keep sharing in-flight work (including the
OnTick prefetch from #23981) without deadlocking callers that hold
`f.mu`.
- The raw state mutex is an `RWMutex`: copies take the read lock,
hashing and branch methods the write lock.
- `postForkchoiceOperations`, block production and forward sync take
private copies of the head state; the rest of their flow is unchanged.
- New metric `caplin_forkchoice_current_state_copy` (copy time under the
fork-choice lock).

Lock order: `f.mu` (read) → raw state mutex.

## Cost

`postForkchoiceOperations` now copies the head state twice per slot: a
private copy under `f.mu.RLock` (~14-15 ms and ~300 MB locally for 1.14M
validators), then the existing copy into the synced-data spare without
`f.mu` (~10-11 ms, reused memory). Both are far below the ~250 ms of a
single copy on main today. Removing the extra copy is left to a
follow-up, after the cost is measured on a Hoodi node.

## Testing

TDD; the failing tests were seen failing first.
- `TestCurrentStateReadersDoNotShareStateWithBlockImport`: readers copy
the head state while `OnBlock` imports its child. Ported to the old API,
it fails under `-race` with data races and a wrong cached state root.
- The two reproduced failure modes from #25111 (writer inside
`hashList.CopyTo`; reader `HashSSZ` inside `hashList.Set` during the
transition) fail on the old code and pass with this change. They need
temporary hooks in `solid/hash_list.go`, which are not committed.
- Deterministic lock tests (no re-locking with a queued writer),
checkpoint singleflight tests, a randomized differential test over every
registry mutator, ptcWindow copy tests and a Gloas reused-spare root
check.
- `go test -race` on the affected packages passes; `go test ./cl/...`
passes except spectest, which needs a mainnet config fixture missing
locally (same on the base).
- Consensus spec tests on local fixtures: the failing set is identical
to the base. The pinned fixtures run in CI.
- `go build ./...` and `make lint` (clean on repeated runs) pass.

## Not included

- Removing the extra head-state copy per slot (see Cost).
- Building the pubkey base lazily for decoded states.
- Compaction of the pubkey delta. Deposits add at most 16 validators per
epoch after Electra; the gauge `beacon_state_pubkey_index_delta_size`
reports its size.
- Pre-existing issues found during review: a late publish of an older
head root can move the synced head back, and `DumpBeaconStateOnDisk`
does not check that the root is still retained.

## Backport

Planned for release/3.8 after this has run on main for a while.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/phase1/core/caches, cl/phase1/core/state, cl/phase1/stages, cl/transition/impl/eth2/statechange: stop sharing the total active balance across branches (#25172)
body:
Fixes #25138.

## Problem

The global active-validators cache stores the total active balance of
epoch E under the key (E, block root at the last slot of E-2). That key
fixes the active set of E, but not the total: the effective balances
that make up the total are written at the E-1 → E boundary from the
balances at the end of E-1.

Two branches that fork during E-1 share the key. After the head precache
stores branch A's total, a state of branch B in epoch E reads A's total
on `SetSlot` at the epoch start, on `Copy`/`CopyInto` and on
`InitBeaconState`. Rewards, justification, slashing penalties, churn
limits and the Gloas builder-payment quorum are then computed with the
wrong total, and B's valid blocks fail the state root check.

## What changed

- The global cache keeps only the active indices, which the key does
identify. The total is removed from the cache value, so `Get` returns
`([]uint64, bool)` and `Put` no longer takes a total.
- Each state sums the effective balances of its own active validators
when its per-state value is empty (`_refreshActiveBalancesIfNeeded` no
longer reads the global cache).
- The head precache (`preCacheActiveValidatorsForEpoch`) stores only the
active set.

Copying the source's per-state total in `CopyInto` was considered and
rejected: the source can be mutated while it is copied, and promoted raw
setters such as `SetValidators` do not invalidate the value.

## Cost

One registry scan per state at the epoch start and on every
`Copy`/`CopyInto`/`InitBeaconState`: about 2-6 ms at 1-2M validators
(measured locally). A full state copy is much more expensive than that
today, so a copy is about 1-2.5 % slower. The canonical head's own
epoch-boundary refresh did not hit the global cache before either, so
that path costs the same.

## Testing

TDD.
`TestTotalActiveBalanceIsNotSharedAcrossBranchesForkedInPreviousEpoch`
builds two branches that share the decision root, fork during E-1 and
get different effective balances through the real epoch transition, then
runs the real precache writer. The precache of one branch must not
change the total that the other branch reads, directly or through
`Copy`, in both directions. On the previous code all four subtests fail
with the other branch's total (2047 ETH expected, 2048 ETH read, and the
reverse); with the change they pass.

`TestLookaheadActiveValidatorsDoNotSupplyTotalBalance` is removed: the
cache value no longer has a total, so the type enforces what it checked.
Other tests only follow the new `Get`/`Put` signatures.

- `go test -race` on `cl/phase1/core/caches`, `cl/phase1/core/state`,
`cl/phase1/stages` and `cl/transition/impl/eth2/statechange` passes.
- `go test ./cl/phase1/... ./cl/transition/...` and `go build ./...`
pass.
- `make lint` (clean on repeated runs) and `make erigon integration`
pass.
- Consensus spec tests on local fixtures: the failing set is identical
to the base. The pinned fixtures run in CI.

## Backport

release/3.8 and release/3.7 have the same cache read
(`cl/phase1/core/state/cache.go`). Planned backport to release/3.8 after
this has run on main for a while.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/transition/impl/eth2/statechange: apply rewards and penalties per delta set as in the spec (#25150)
body:
Stacked on #25144, which restructured the same function. Please review
and merge #25144 first; the diff of this PR is only the last commit.

## Problem

The post-Altair rewards and penalties step sums all flag rewards and
penalties and the inactivity penalty into one net delta per validator
and applies it with a single clamp at zero.

The spec applies the delta sets in order (source, target and head flag
deltas, then inactivity penalties). For each set it calls
`increase_balance` with the reward and then `decrease_balance` with the
penalty, and `decrease_balance` clamps at zero. When a penalty is larger
than the current balance, the results differ. Example: balance 10,
source penalty 15, target reward 8. The spec gives 8; the net delta
gives 3.

On real chains this is very likely unreachable: active unslashed
validators are ejected long before a single penalty is larger than their
balance, and slashed validators get no rewards, so they only see
decreases, where both orders give the same result. This PR makes the
code match the spec anyway.

## What changed

- The parallel loop reads the current balance (read only; no balance is
written during the parallel phase) and applies the rewards and penalties
in spec order, clamping at zero after each penalty.
- The resulting balances are written serially in eligible-index order,
as in #25144, and a compute error still writes no balance.
- When no clamp is hit, the result is the same as before.

## Testing

TDD. `TestProcessRewardsAndPenaltiesClampsEachDeltaSet`: a validator
with balance 1 that misses source and head and hits target ends with
exactly the target reward. It fails on the previous code (balance 0) and
passes with the change.

- `go test -race ./cl/transition/... ./cl/phase1/core/state/...` passes.
- `go test ./cl/phase1/... ./cl/transition/...` and `go build ./...`
pass.
- `make lint` (clean on repeated runs) and `make erigon integration`
pass.
- Mainnet `epoch_processing`, `rewards` and `sanity` consensus spec
tests, phase0 to gloas: 2119 pass, 0 fail on both the base and this
change, run locally on the v1.7.0-beta.2 fixtures (the pinned beta.4
fixtures run in CI). The spec fixtures do not reach this case, so they
also pass on the previous code; the new unit test is the regression
guard.
- `BenchmarkEpochProcessing/RewardsAndPenalties` (200k validators):
median ~3.25 ms → ~2.48 ms, same allocations.

## Not included

The phase0 path is unchanged. It also differs from the spec (penalties
are subtracted without a clamp, and the inclusion-delay and proposer
rewards are added after the penalties), but only when a penalty exceeds
the balance, which is also very likely unreachable.

## Backport

Not planned for release/3.8: the case is very likely unreachable on real
chains.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/transition, cl/phase1/core/state: verify Gloas bid and payload attestation signatures in the block batch (#25192)
body:
## What and why

Part of #25120 (item 4).

Gloas block processing verified the execution payload bid signature and
every payload attestation signature one by one, outside the block's
batched BLS check. This PR adds them to the existing
`bls.VerifyMultipleSignatures` batch in `machine.ProcessBlock`, the same
way proposer slashings and voluntary exits already work.

## Changes

- `machine.ProcessBlock` adds the bid signature to the batch (not for
self-build bids).
- `machine.ProcessOperations` adds one entry per payload attestation:
the signature, the signing root, and the aggregated public key of the
attesting PTC members.
- `impl.ProcessExecutionPayloadBid` and `impl.ProcessPayloadAttestation`
no longer verify signatures. All other checks stay in place.
- `state.IsValidIndexedPayloadAttestation` becomes
`state.IndexedPayloadAttestationSignatureSet`, and the bid signature
helper moves to `state.ExecutionPayloadBidSignatureSet`. Both return
signature-set inputs instead of verifying.
- `ErrInvalidExecutionPayloadBid` moves from `impl/eth2` to `machine`.
Block production uses it to evict a bad bid, as before.
- The spectest handlers for `execution_payload_bid` and
`payload_attestation` verify the signature after the impl call, so the
operation tests still cover signature failures.
- `CLAUDE.md` spec maps updated.

## Behaviour notes

- Accepted and rejected blocks are unchanged. Only the place where the
signatures are checked moves.
- Error classification for bid eviction: when the batch fails and the
block has a non-self-build bid, the bid signature is verified alone. If
it is invalid, the error wraps `ErrInvalidExecutionPayloadBid` and
production evicts the bid. If the bid is valid, the batch error is
returned as before, so an invalid payload attestation or RANDAO
signature does not evict a good bid.
- Known, accepted case: if an operation fails before the batch runs, an
invalid bid signature is not seen, so production does not evict that
bid. The block is rejected either way.
`TestProcessBlockEarlierOperationFailureMasksInvalidBidSignature` pins
this.
- The PTC signing domain still uses
`compute_epoch_at_slot(attestation.data.slot)`, as in the spec.
- Aggregated PTC public keys go through the existing BLS public key
cache.

## Benchmark

`BenchmarkProcessOperationsPayloadAttestationSignatures` (4 payload
attestations, 512 validators, one extra signature in the batch), `-count
5`, Apple M5 Pro. The base run uses the same benchmark file on
`origin/main`.

| | ns/op (median) | B/op | allocs/op |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| base | 5,308,567 | ~210,100 | 452 |
| this PR | 2,661,125 | ~173,250 | 418 |

About 2x faster for this workload.

## Tests and spectests

- New `cl/transition/machine/block_signatures_test.go`: invalid bid and
payload attestation signatures are rejected; an invalid bid takes
precedence over an invalid payload attestation for classification;
self-build does not classify as a bid error; duplicate PTC members;
infinite or undecodable keys and signatures; pre-Gloas and Gloas batch
errors are preserved; the masking case above.
- New handler tests: an invalid bid signature is evicted through the
machine path, and a valid bid is kept when only a payload attestation
signature is invalid.
- `go test ./cl/transition/... ./cl/phase1/core/state/...
./cl/beacon/handler/...` pass.
- Consensus spectests v1.7.0-beta.4, `-run '/mainnet/(gloas|fulu)/'`:
2932 pass, 0 fail.
- `make lint` clean, `make erigon integration` build.

## TDD

The new machine and handler tests pin the batch behaviour and the bid
eviction classification for the moved checks. The helper renames in
`state` and the move of `ErrInvalidExecutionPayloadBid` are refactors;
the existing tests and the spectests cover them.

author: Kewei
subject: cl: batch-verify gossip PTC signatures and re-check failed batches in parallel (#25198)
body:
Part of #25120 (item 3).

## What and why

Each gossip PTC message (`payload_attestation_message`) was verified on
its own with `bls.VerifyAggregate`. With up to 512 messages per slot,
that is about 0.6–0.7 ms of CPU per message. This PR sends gossip PTC
signatures through `BatchSignatureVerifier`, which verifies them in
randomized batches.

A failed batch is expensive: `handleIncorrectSignatures` re-checked
every entry one by one on the queue goroutine, so one invalid signature
in a 50-entry batch cost about 50 serial verifications before any waiter
got its result. This PR also makes that fallback parallel, which helps
every queue, not only PTC.

The PR has two commits:
1. `cl/phase1/network/services: re-check failed batch entries in
parallel`
2. `cl: batch-verify gossip PTC signatures`

## Changes

### Parallel fallback (first commit)

- The entries of a failed batch are verified in parallel. Callbacks,
error reports and the peer ban still run in the original input order,
after all checks finish.
- One `semaphore.Weighted` per verifier limits the fallback work. Its
size is `GOMAXPROCS` at construction, and it is shared by all queues and
by `ImmediateVerification`.
- Each entry takes a weight of `min(len(signatures), budget)`, so an
entry with more signatures than the budget can still run.

### PTC batch verification (second commit)

- `OnGossipPayloadAttestationMessage` takes a
`PayloadAttestationSignatureVerifier`. When it is nil, the signature is
verified immediately as before. The signature is still the last check,
and the vote is applied only after it passes.
- `payloadAttestationService` passes the batch verifier for gossip
messages only. REST and pending messages are still verified immediately.
- A dedicated PTC queue in `BatchSignatureVerifier` flushes every 20 ms
instead of the default 50 ms. PTC votes are due at 75% of the slot, so a
shorter wait keeps them closer to the deadline.
- **Per-slot fallback:** after the batch verifier reports an invalid
signature for a slot, later gossip messages for that slot are verified
immediately. The marker keeps the highest such slot, so a late failure
report for an older slot cannot cancel the fallback for a newer one.
Cancellation and shutdown (`ErrIgnore`) do not set it.
- An invalid signature is still REJECT with one peer ban.

## Trade-offs

- Without forged signatures, a PTC vote waits up to one batch interval:
p50 about 13 ms and max about 30 ms in the harness below, compared with
about 1–2 ms before.
- One forged signature makes its batch fail, so the honest votes in it
wait for the parallel fallback. With the per-slot fallback, this costs
at most the batches that are already queued when the first failure is
reported, once per slot. If all votes of a slot arrive within about one
batch round-trip, the fallback helps little for that slot.
- `validationAdmission` (512) is held while a message waits for its
batch, so during a burst, local REST submissions can wait longer
(measured 60–170 ms).
- An attacker who sends invalid signatures can now use all cores for
fallback checks, not about one core per queue. The total work is the
same as before.
- At `GOMAXPROCS=1`, nothing runs in parallel, and the mean waiter
latency for a failed batch is about twice as high: before, an early
entry got its result as soon as its own check finished.
- `Acquire` does not use the verifier context. A wait is bounded by the
running checks, also at shutdown.

## Benchmark

All numbers are from an Apple M5 Pro (18 cores).

`BenchmarkBatchSignatureVerifierFallback`, a 50-entry batch with one
invalid signature, base vs this PR at the same `GOMAXPROCS`:

| GOMAXPROCS | base | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 47.8 ms | 48.6 ms |
| 4 | 43.7 ms | 18.2 ms |
| 8 | 45.4 ms | 11.7 ms |
| 18 | 45.6 ms | 9.3 ms |

The all-valid case is unchanged. Total CPU time for the failed case is
4–7% higher.

PTC cases of the same benchmark, concurrent `individual` baseline vs
batch, time per message:

| Case | `-cpu 1` batch | `-cpu 1` individual | `-cpu 8` batch | `-cpu
8` individual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all valid | 313 µs | 596 µs | 78 µs | 90 µs |
| 1 invalid in batch | 944 µs | 595 µs | 169 µs | 88 µs |

Latency harness, 512 PTC messages arriving at random times within 1 s,
GOMAXPROCS 18, all valid: p50 / max latency 13.5 / 26 ms at 20 ms, 29.9
/ 59 ms at 50 ms, 1.2 / 3 ms for immediate verification. CPU per run:
534 ms, 387 ms and 758 ms.

The "1 invalid" rows were measured before the per-slot fallback; with
it, only the first batches of a slot can fail.

## Tests

Parallel fallback:
- `TestBatchSignatureVerifierChecksFailedBatchEntriesConcurrently`: the
checks of a failed batch run at the same time, and callbacks still run
in input order when the checks finish in a different order.
- `TestBatchSignatureVerifierSharesFallbackConcurrencyBudget`: two
failed batches on different queues together never run more checks at
once than the shared budget allows.
- `TestBatchSignatureVerifierCapsFallbackWeightAtBudget`: an entry with
more signatures than the budget does not block forever.

PTC batch verification:
- `TestOnGossipPayloadAttestationMessageUsesInjectedSignatureVerifier`,
`TestOnGossipPayloadAttestationMessageInjectedVerifierErrorRejects`:
fork choice uses the injected verifier, and its error is a REJECT, not
an IGNORE.
- `TestVerifyPayloadAttestationBatchMatchesSinglePath`: the batch path
accepts and rejects the same signatures as the immediate path.
- `TestBatchSignatureVerifierUsesPayloadAttestationFlushInterval`: the
PTC queue flushes after exactly 20 ms, all other queues after 50 ms,
also after a full batch.
- `TestPayloadAttestationServiceSelectsSignatureVerifierByIngress`:
gossip uses the batch verifier; REST and pending do not.
- `TestPayloadAttestationServiceBatchSignatureOutcomes`: invalid gossip
is rejected, valid gossip is accepted, an invalid batch result switches
only its slot to immediate verification, a raw fallback error also does,
an older failure does not replace a newer fallback slot, and
cancellation is a retryable IGNORE that does not set the fallback.

The concurrency and timing tests use `testing/synctest`, so a regression
fails fast instead of hanging.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/cltypes/solid, cl/phase1/forkchoice: cache Gloas payload roots and hash them outside the fork-choice lock (#25193)
body:
Part of #25120 (item 2: the uncached payload hash; the disk write under
the lock is not in this PR).

## What and why

In Gloas, the execution payload uses progressive SSZ lists for
`transactions` and `block_access_list`.
`TransactionsSSZ.HashSSZProgressive` and
`ByteListSSZ.HashSSZProgressive` did not cache their roots, so every
`HashSSZ` call on the payload re-hashed every transaction and the whole
block access list. `applyEnvelope` hashed the payload while it held
`f.mu`, so this work blocked every other fork-choice reader and writer.

This PR caches the two progressive roots and computes them in
`applyEnvelope` before it takes `f.mu`. The hash calls under the lock
then read the cache.

## Changes

- `TransactionsSSZ` and `ByteListSSZ` get a separate progressive-root
cache, `progressiveRoot *atomic.Pointer[[32]byte]`. Every mutation
(`DecodeSSZ`, `UnmarshalJSON`, `SetBytes`, constructors) installs a new
pointer, so a hash that loaded the old pointer can only fill the old,
discarded cache. Hashing while another goroutine mutates the same object
is still a data race, as before. The cache is filled with
`CompareAndSwap(nil, ...)`, so concurrent hashers are safe.
- The legacy `TransactionsSSZ.root` cache is unchanged and stays
separate from the progressive root.
- `applyEnvelope` warms the payload root caches before `f.mu.Lock()`,
for both `validatePayload` values. It skips the warm-up when the
envelope is already stored (`HasEnvelope`), because that path returns
early without hashing.
- The transaction-aliasing contract is unchanged: `UnderlyngReference()`
callers only read the slices, and the existing legacy root cache already
relies on the same contract.

## Benchmark

`BenchmarkEth1BlockHashSSZGloas` in
`cl/cltypes/eth1_block_bench_test.go`, `-count=5`, Apple M5 Pro, `main`
vs this PR, runs interleaved. The machine was under load, so the cold
numbers are noisy (the cold difference is not significant, p=0.690).

| Case | main | this PR | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 300 tx / 100 KB BAL, cold | 543.5 µs, 430.3 KiB, 1534 allocs | 479.7
µs, 430.3 KiB, 1536 allocs | ~ |
| 300 tx / 100 KB BAL, warm | 534.1 µs, 430.3 KiB, 1534 allocs | 1.92
µs, 2.4 KiB, 20 allocs | -99.6% |
| 1500 tx / 400 KB BAL, cold | 2.32 ms, 1.87 MiB, 7537 allocs | 2.08 ms,
1.87 MiB, 7539 allocs | ~ |
| 1500 tx / 400 KB BAL, warm | 2.11 ms, 1.87 MiB, 7537 allocs | 1.99 µs,
2.4 KiB, 20 allocs | -99.9% |

"Cold" hashes a freshly decoded payload; "warm" hashes the same payload
again. On `main` both cases do the full work.

## Tests

- `TestTransactionsSSZProgressiveRootMemoized`,
`TestByteListSSZProgressiveRootMemoized`: a second progressive hash
allocates nothing, so it is served from the cache.
- `TestTransactionsSSZMutationInvalidatesProgressiveRoot`,
`TestByteListSSZMutationInvalidatesProgressiveRoot`: after `DecodeSSZ`
(also empty input), `UnmarshalJSON` or `SetBytes`, the root matches a
fresh object with the new data, not the cached old root.
- `TestTransactionsSSZDecodeFailureInvalidatesProgressiveRoot`: a
`DecodeSSZ` that fails after it has partly replaced the data still drops
the old cached root.
- `TestTransactionsSSZLegacyAndProgressiveRootsAreSeparate`: the legacy
and progressive roots do not overwrite each other, in either call order.
- `TestTransactionsSSZProgressiveRootConcurrent`,
`TestByteListSSZProgressiveRootConcurrent`: concurrent first hashes all
return the correct root; with `go test -race ./cl/cltypes/solid/` they
guard the cache against data races.
- `TestApplyEnvelopeWarmsPayloadRootCachesBeforeLock`: with `f.mu` held
by the test, `applyEnvelope` fills both payload root caches before it
gets the lock, for `validatePayload` true and false.
- `TestApplyEnvelopeSkipsPayloadRootCacheWarmupForStoredEnvelope`: for
an envelope that is already stored, `applyEnvelope` does not hash the
payload.

## TDD note

The cache behavior was driven by the `solid` tests above. The warm-up
line in `applyEnvelope` adds no logic beyond what the two forkchoice
tests pin. The benchmark adds no production logic; it only provides the
numbers above.

author: awskii
subject: cl/phase1/forkchoice: keep pre-Gloas get_head vote weights across calls (#24985)
body:
Before Gloas, every `get_head` recompute sums all validators' latest
messages under `f.mu`. On a mainnet tip node that is 40–82 ms between
execution and the FCU, about twice per slot. Gloas already keeps weights
incrementally (`gloasWeightTree`), so this covers mainnet until
Glamsterdam.

## Changes
- `voteTally` keeps per-root vote weights across calls: a rebuild when
the justified checkpoint state changes, otherwise only validators whose
message or equivocation changed.
- Proposer boost, `accountWeights` and the auxiliary-state path are
unchanged.

## Numbers
Mainnet tip node (`awskii/v3-commitment`), 3 interleaved 40-min arms per
binary:

| | base | this |
|---|---|---|
| execution done → FCU p50 | 107 ms | 41 ms (p 4e-5) |
| FCU → head updated, after the reply | 5 ms | 8 ms |

The +3 ms is Caplin's head-state copy, no longer queued behind the
recount, overlapping the flush.

---------

Co-authored-by: Alex Sharov <AskAlexSharov@gmail.com>

author: Kewei
subject: cl/cltypes: cache the Gloas block body root by its encoding (#25191)
body:
Part of #25120 (item 6).

## What and why

The node computes the root of a Gloas block body about 14 times for each
block it imports from gossip. Each time, it hashes the full body again.
This PR caches the root for Gloas and later bodies. Fulu and earlier
bodies are not changed.

## Design

`BeaconBody.HashSSZ` encodes the body and compares the encoding with the
cached one:

- byte-equal: it returns the cached root;
- different, or nothing cached yet: it hashes the body and stores
`(encoding, root)` in an `*atomic.Pointer` that `NewBeaconBody`
allocates.

Why byte-equality and not a dirty flag: the body fields are exported and
mutable, nested values such as `AggregationBits` can change in place,
and block production copies bodies by value. A flag cannot see these
changes, but the encoding always does. Encoding is much cheaper than
hashing.

- Struct copies share the pointer. A changed copy encodes differently,
so it can only miss and store its own entry. It never returns a wrong
root.
- Bodies built with a struct literal have a nil pointer and are hashed
without the cache.
- The capacity hint for the encoding buffer uses the length of the
cached encoding.
- Concurrent callers are safe: the entry is immutable and is swapped
atomically.

## Cost

Each cached body keeps its encoding, about 41 KB for a full mainnet
body. That is about 41 MB at 1,000 unfinalized blocks and about 410 MB
at 10,000.

## Benchmark

`BenchmarkGloasBodyHashSSZ` in `cl/cltypes`, mainnet config, 8 full
attestations and 4 full payload attestations, Apple M5 Pro, `-count 5`,
run twice. The machine was under load, so the table shows the fastest
run of each case.

| case | ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline: `hashSSZGloas()`, uncached (same as `main`) | 76,231 |
130,528 | 281 |
| miss: encode + hash + store | 80,884 | 269,144 | 445 |
| hit: encode + compare | 5,278 | 48,440 | 161 |

The benchmark file does not compile on `main` because it uses the new
cache field, so the baseline calls `hashSSZGloas()` directly. On `main`,
that is what `HashSSZ` runs for a Gloas body. A miss costs about 6% more
than the baseline. A hit is about 14x faster.

## Tests

`cl/cltypes/beacon_body_root_cache_test.go`:

- a cache hit returns the stored entry, and a changed field replaces it;
- an in-place change of nested `AggregationBits` changes the root;
- changing a struct copy changes only the copy's root, and the original
body still returns its own correct root;
- version gate: Fulu does not cache, Gloas and Heze do;
- a nil cache pointer falls back to hashing without the cache;
- `TestGloasBodyRootCacheConcurrent` checks concurrent callers. It is a
`-race` guard: without the race detector it only checks that every root
is correct.

Every root is also checked against an uncached `hashSSZGloas()`.

## Known limits

Two cases give equal encodings but different roots. In both, the cache
could return the root of the other value. Neither can be reached,
because decode, JSON parsing and block production validation reject
both:

- `CommitteeBits` nil compared with a 0-bit vector;
- payload-attestation bitvectors with a non-standard width.

## Follow-up

`EncodingSizeSSZ` undercounts Gloas bodies by 396 bytes. Here it affects
only the first capacity hint. It also backs the decode lower-bound
check, so it needs a separate change.

## TDD note

The tests pin the cache behavior: a hit, invalidation after a change,
struct copies, the version gate and concurrent callers. The branch was
developed in review rounds and then squashed, so the commit does not
show a separate red step. I checked this with a mutation: when the cache
returns the stored root without comparing the encoding, the hit,
nested-change and struct-copy tests fail.

author: Kewei
subject: cl: learn attached validators from subscriptions and proposer preferences (#25183)
body:
## Problem

Caplin learns which validators are attached to it only from `POST
/eth/v1/validator/prepare_beacon_proposer`. Teku 26.10.1 and Prysm
v7.3.0 validator clients stop sending that call once Gloas is active
(Teku at its first Gloas slot), because signed proposer preferences
replace it. When Caplin restarts in Gloas while such a validator client
keeps running, the in-memory set is empty, and validators added after
Gloas are never added to it. For such a Caplin node:

- validator custody is never raised (custody is recomputed in `OnBlock`
only when the set is non-empty; on a test network it stayed at 4 custody
groups instead of 96);
- gossip aggregates skip signature verification and return `ErrIgnore`,
so they are not pooled, relayed or applied to fork choice, and blocks
are packed from a smaller attestation pool (on the test network 4 to 10
attestations instead of about 390);
- gossip sync committee contributions are ignored;
- block production falls back to the zero fee recipient for slots
without a per-slot preference.

Lighthouse keeps sending `prepare_beacon_proposer` after Gloas and is
not affected.

## What changed

- `ValidatorParams` keeps a set of attached validator indices, and
`GetValidators` returns it. `SetFeeRecipient` also adds the index to
this set, so every `prepare_beacon_proposer` registration stays
attached. Adding an attached validator changes neither `GetFeeRecipient`
nor `Generation`.
- `POST /eth/v1/validator/beacon_committee_subscriptions` records every
validator index in a non-empty request before subscribing, so it records
them also when the node is still syncing (503). `POST
/eth/v1/validator/sync_committee_subscriptions` records the indices of a
request that passes validation, also for entries that have already
expired. Like `prepare_beacon_proposer`, neither endpoint checks the
validator index. Prysm also learns attached validators from beacon
committee subscriptions, but only after a successful request, for
indices in its head state, and for one hour.
- Once the wall clock is in Gloas, `POST
/eth/v1/validator/proposer_preferences` stores the fee recipient of each
item whose signature is valid for the validator's key in the head state.
It does this also when gossip validation ignores the item, for example a
slot that already passed. Before Gloas, `prepare_beacon_proposer` stays
the only source, so preferences sent in the epoch before the fork do not
replace the registered fee recipient. `POST
/eth/v1/beacon/pool/proposer_preferences` and preferences received over
gossip do not record anything. The response, gossip validation, the pool
and publishing do not change. Teku also fills its prepared proposers
from the preferences its validator client submits after Gloas. The
signature check is shared with gossip validation
(`VerifyProposerPreferencesSignature`).

## Tests

- `TestAttachedValidatorsAreIndependentFromFeeRecipients`: an
attached-only validator is listed once, also when it later gets a fee
recipient. A validator registered only through `SetFeeRecipient` is
listed. Adding an attached validator creates no fee recipient and does
not change the generation.
-
`TestBeaconCommitteeSubscriptionRecordsAttachedValidatorsBeforeSubscribing`:
a batch for validators 7 and 8 records both when the first subscription
returns `ErrNotSynced`.
- `TestSyncCommitteeSubscriptionRecordsAttachedValidatorWhenExpired`.
`TestSyncCommitteeSubscriptionRejectsInvalidIndices` now also checks
that an invalid batch records nothing.
- `TestAggregateAndProofIsVerifiedWhenTheNodeHasValidators/attached`: an
attached-only validator makes the aggregate verified and pooled instead
of ignored.
- `TestOnBlockUpdatesCustodyForAttachedValidatorWithoutFeeRecipient`: an
attached-only validator makes `OnBlock` update validator custody.
-
`TestPostProposerPreferencesRecordsFeeRecipientFromValidPastPreference`:
a signed preference for a past slot, posted to the validator endpoint,
sets the fee recipient that block production's resolver
(`feeRecipientForProposal`) then returns for a later slot. An invalid
signature, a missing head state, an unknown validator, the beacon pool
endpoint and a wall clock before Gloas store no fee recipient.

The new attached-only, subscription and preference positive cases failed
before the fix; the fee-recipient cases and the negative cases guard
existing and new code. Each of these mutations makes at least one test
fail: removing a recording call, moving the committee recording into the
subscription loop, moving the sync committee recording before validation
or after the expiry check, not adding fee-recipient registrations to the
attached set, skipping the signature check, recording from the beacon
pool endpoint, or dropping the Gloas check.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/das, cl/persistence/beacon_indicies, cl/phase1/forkchoice: persist the highest custody group count across restarts (#25187)
body:
Part of #23566

## Problem

consensus-specs `fulu/validator.md` says a node SHOULD keep advertising
the previous (highest) `custody_group_count`, and that this value SHOULD
persist across node restarts. Caplin keeps it only in memory:
`NewPeerDasState` starts at `CUSTODY_REQUIREMENT`, so after a restart a
node that had raised its count advertises the minimum again. In a
devnet, a standalone Caplin with 96 attached validators advertised
`cgc=96`, was restarted, and came back with `cgc=4` (column subnets 96
-> 8).

## What changed

- `beacon_indicies`: `WriteHighestCustodyGroupCount` /
`ReadHighestCustodyGroupCount` store the count under a new key in the
existing `DbInfo` table of the Caplin indexing DB. For any valid custody
group count, a write never lowers the stored value.
- `peerdas.UpdateValidatorsCustody` persists the count when the
advertised count increases. `NewPeerDas` now takes a `kv.RwDB` for this.
- `peerdas.Start` reads the stored count and raises the advertised count
before it subscribes to column subnets. This runs after
`SetLocalNodeID`, so the raise also updates the ENR `cgc` entry, and the
subscriptions, the ENR and the metadata use the stored value from then
on. Both the standalone and the embedded Caplin go through
`RunCaplinService`, so both are covered. Archive mode still subscribes
to all subnets.
- `PeerDasState.RaiseAdvertisedCgc` raises only the advertised count.
`SetCustodyGroupCount` uses the same code and still sets the real count.
- `PeerDasState.GetMyCustodyColumns` now computes and caches the custody
columns under the cgc read lock. Before, a read that started before a
raise could store the columns for the old count after the raise had
cleared the cache, and the node then subscribed to and checked the old
columns while it advertised the new count. The restore in `Start` adds
one more raise at startup, so this change goes with it.
- `OnBlock` now calls `UpdateValidatorsCustody` after it releases the
fork-choice lock. The call writes the indexing DB now, and the
fork-choice stage holds an indexing-DB write tx while it waits for that
lock, so the write must not happen under it. Concurrent `OnBlock` calls
can now reach `UpdateValidatorsCustody` in a different order than they
took the lock. The advertised and the stored counts only take the
maximum, so when the DB writes succeed the order does not change them.
The real count can reflect an older block until the next
`UpdateValidatorsCustody` call, but nothing reads it in production.

The ENR seed in `cl/p2p` is unchanged. Discovery and the sentinel
metadata handler start before `peerdas.Start`, so for a short time
during startup the ENR and the metadata still show
`CUSTODY_REQUIREMENT`. When `Start` raises the count, the ENR gets the
stored value with a higher sequence number.

A failed DB write or read is only logged. A failed write is not retried
until the advertised count increases again, so after a restart the node
can come back with an older stored value. A failed read in `Start` is
not retried for that run.

Out of scope, for later PRs:
- `earliest_available_slot` following the custody group count change (a
later sentence in the same section of the spec). For this reason this PR
does not close #23566.
- Backfill of columns when the custody group count increases.
- #24787.

## Tests

- `TestPeerDasRestoresHighestCustodyGroupCount`: raises the count to 96
through `UpdateValidatorsCustody` on an in-memory MDBX test DB (the
chain-DB tables, which the Caplin DB also uses), then builds a new
`PeerDasState` and `peerdas` on the same open DB and calls `Start`. It
checks that the advertised count and the ENR `cgc` entry are 96. Before
the fix it failed with `expected: 0x60, actual: 0x4`.
- `TestPeerDasStartWithoutStoredCustodyGroupCountKeepsRequirement`: with
nothing stored, the count stays at `CUSTODY_REQUIREMENT`.
- `TestHighestCustodyGroupCountNeverDecreases`,
`TestHighestCustodyGroupCountDefaultsToZero`: storage semantics.
- `TestRaiseAdvertisedCgcDoesNotChangeRealCgc`: raising to 96 updates
the ENR and keeps the real count; a later lower value leaves the
advertised count and the ENR unchanged.
- `TestRaiseAdvertisedCgcIsNotLostToAConcurrentCustodyColumnsRead`: in
1000 rounds, four goroutines call `GetMyCustodyColumns` on a new state
while the main goroutine raises the count to 128; a final call must then
return 128 columns. Before the fix it failed in 30 of 30 local runs
(GOMAXPROCS 2, 4 and the default) with `should have 128 item(s), but has
8`. The test is probabilistic: in local runs with GOMAXPROCS=1 it did
not catch the old code.
- `TestOnBlockUpdatesValidatorsCustodyWithoutForkChoiceLock`: fails if
`UpdateValidatorsCustody` is called under the fork-choice lock.

The new non-error branches were mutation-checked locally: removing one
makes one of these tests fail. The DB error paths in `Start`,
`UpdateValidatorsCustody` and the storage accessors have no tests. The
restart test reuses one open DB; it does not close and reopen MDBX.

author: Kewei
subject: execution/builder, txnprovider: stop waiting for the parent block once a payload is collected (#25082)
body:
## Problem

`engine_getPayload` collects a payload through `GetAssembledBlock`,
which calls `BlockBuilder.Stop`. `Stop` sets the interrupt flag and then
waits until the build function returns or the caller's context ends. The
build reads that flag only between transaction provider calls.

During transaction selection, `TxPool.best` waits until the pool has
seen the build's parent block. If a forkchoice update moves the head
below that parent after the build has started, the pool's
`lastSeenBlock` drops below the parent and the build parks in that wait.
Only a new block or the end of the build context wakes it. While the
node runs, the build context ends only on `Discard`. The max-build-time
watchdog calls `Stop` first and calls `Discard` only after the stop
grace of half a slot. So `getPayload` blocks until the pool sees a block
at the parent's height again, the grace runs out, or its own context
ends. In the last two cases it gets no payload. The shutter provider has
its own parent-block wait with the same effect. It is bounded by one
slot, and when that deadline passes the whole build fails.

We saw this on a local Gloas shadow fork. 9 ms after a build started, a
forkchoice update moved the EL head one block back. `getPayloadV6`
arrived about 12 s later and waited until the head was back at the
parent, about 9 s later. The consensus client gave up after 2 s and the
slot was missed.

A smaller source of latency: between provider polls, the selection loop
sleeps for 50 ms with `time.Sleep`, and `Stop` cannot wake it.

The spec says that for `engine_getPayloadV1` the client software MUST
return the most recent version of the payload that is available in the
build process at the time of the call, and gives the method a 1 s
timeout.

## Fix

- New provide option `txnprovider.WithParentBlockWaitStop(stop <-chan
struct{})`. Once `stop` is closed, a provider that waits for the parent
block stops waiting and returns no transactions and no error. Other
waits are not affected.
- txpool: the goroutine in `best` that already wakes the condition
variable on context cancellation also wakes it when `stop` is closed.
The wait loop then returns no transactions and logs at Debug. A call
that starts with `stop` already closed does not start that goroutine:
the wait loop sees the closed channel itself, and the goroutine would
only take `p.lock` to broadcast for nothing.
- shutter: the parent-block wait context is cancelled when `stop` is
closed. If the tracker has still not seen the parent, `ProvideTxns`
returns no transactions, logs at Debug and counts it in the new
`shutter_parent_block_wait_stopped` counter. If it has, the call goes on
as before. The stop is read from the channel after the wait, not
inferred from the error type, and the goroutine that watches it is
started only when a stop channel is given and ends as soon as the wait
returns.
- shutter: when the one-slot parent-block deadline passes and the
caller's context is still live, `ProvideTxns` now falls back to the base
txn provider and logs at Warn (and counts `shutter_parent_block_missed`,
as before), like the other degraded exits of the function (unknown eon,
decryption-keys timeout). Before, the deadline error failed the whole
build, so a `getPayload` near the end of the call's slot, or a shutter
block listener that lags, gave no payload at all. `BlockTracker.Wait`
now also checks the caller's cancellation before the tracker's stopped
state, so a stop-driven cancellation that races a tracker shutdown is
reported as a cancellation. For this, `BlockTracker.Wait` now decides
its result from the tracker state: a cancellation that races a parent
already there returns success, and one for a parent not yet seen always
returns the context error (before, the waiter goroutine could finish
first and `Wait` returned `nil`). `Wait` also broadcasts under the
condition lock and joins its waiter, so a cancellation can no longer be
lost between the waiter's check and `Cond.Wait`. The decryption-keys
wait is not affected on purpose. The Gnosis shutter spec says the
proposer holds off until it receives the decryption keys, so ending that
wait at `getPayload` would drop the slot's encrypted transactions.
- `BlockBuilder.Stop` closes two channels, once. `stopped` closes at
once and ends the 50 ms idle wait of the selection loop.
`parentBlockWaitStopped` closes `parentBlockWaitGrace` (500 ms) later,
and the selection loop passes it to every provider call as
`WithParentBlockWaitStop`. This also covers the max-build-time watchdog,
which calls `Stop`. The channels reach the selection loop through the
build context (`stopSignalsOf`), so `BlockBuilderFunc` keeps its
signature.
- Packing and finalization still use the build context, and `Discard`
works as before.

A provider call that starts after the stop, when the parent is already
seen, still returns transactions as before. So the packing after a stop
does not change.

Why the grace: if `getPayload` arrives right after a `forkchoiceUpdated`
that moved the head, the txpool may not have processed the new head yet.
On `main`, the build waits until the pool catches up and then packs
transactions. Ending the wait at once made such a payload empty. CI
showed this: `TestAssembleBlockGasOverflow` and
`TestEngineApiUnwindToSnapshotBoundaryPreservesDeletedSlots` call
`getPayload` right after the forkchoice update and failed on slow
runners with blocks that had no transactions. With the grace, a pool
that catches up within 500 ms after the stop still fills the payload, as
on `main`. A pool that stays behind the parent costs at most 500 ms
more, plus finalization, instead of an unbounded wait. 500 ms is half of
the Engine API's 1 s `getPayload` timeout.

Trade-off for the max-build-time watchdog: it calls the same `Stop`, so
a build that is still parked in the parent-block wait when its budget
ends now finishes 500 ms later with the transactions it has, possibly
none, and a later `getPayload` gets that block. On `main` the build kept
waiting for up to the stop grace (half a slot) and could still pack a
full block if the pool caught up in that time; otherwise it was
discarded and `getPayload` got no payload. The budget ends a third of a
slot into the payload's own slot (`buildDuration`), so a `getPayload`
that arrives after the watchdog fired is already late. I kept one grace
for both cases rather than adding a `Stop` argument for it.

I did not cancel the provider call's context on stop, and treat that
cancellation as the end of selection, although that would be a smaller
change in the builder. It would also end the shutter decryption-keys
wait. And every txpool call made after the stop would fail, because
`BeginRo` checks the context, so selection would end with only what had
been collected before the stop. For a `getPayload` that arrives right
after `forkchoiceUpdated`, that can be nothing, although the pool has
transactions. Without that extra handling, the cancellation error would
make the whole build fail.

## Remaining latency (not changed here)

- `BlockAssembler.AddTransactions` (`execution/exec/block_assembler.go`)
keeps packing for 500 ms after the stop request ("ensure we run for at
least 500ms after the request to stop comes in from GetPayload"). The
timer is checked only between transactions, and it starts again in each
`AddTransactions` call. So the packing after a stop can take longer than
500 ms, for example while the provider keeps returning full batches. I
leave this trade-off to the owners of the builder.
- Finalization (commitment, sealing) and a single heavy transaction
still add to the latency.

## Relation to #22835

#22835 fixed a deadlock in the same txpool wait: `Stop` now honours the
caller's context, so a cancelled or expired `getPayload` returns an
error and releases the execution semaphore. The consensus client still
gets no payload in that case. With this change, a `getPayload` with a
live context gets the payload that has been built so far.

## Tests

Each new test was written before the production change it covers, and
failed for the expected reason:

- `TestGetAssembledBlockDoesNotWaitForTxPoolBehindParent`
(`execution/execmodule`): the existing `rewindingTxnProvider` seam moves
the txpool head back to the block before the parent when selection
starts. `GetAssembledBlock` with a live context and a 5 s deadline must
return a payload built on the original parent. On `main`: `context
deadline exceeded`.
- `TestGetAssembledBlockIncludesTxnsOnceTxPoolCatchesUpSoonAfterStop`
(`execution/execmodule`): the same seam, with two pending transactions.
The build runs in a `testing/synctest` bubble, and the txpool head goes
back to the parent once the stopped build is parked in the parent-block
wait, so the 500 ms grace has not passed yet. The payload must contain
both transactions. With the grace set to 0: 0 transactions (10 of 10
runs).
- `TestStopWakesBuilderWaitingForMoreTransactions`
(`execution/execmodule`): runs in a `testing/synctest` bubble. The
provider runs dry, and `Stop` must return without any time passing.
Without the idle-wait change, fake time advanced by exactly 50 ms.
- `TestProvideTxnsReturnsNothingOnceTheParentBlockWaitIsStopped`
(`txnprovider/txpool`): a call parked in the parent-block wait returns
no transactions and no error once the stop channel is closed. With the
option added but not yet honoured by the txpool, it was still waiting
after 5 s.
- `TestPoolProvideTxnsReturnsNothingOnceTheParentBlockWaitIsStopped`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): the same for the shutter parent-block wait.
With the option not yet honoured by shutter, it was still waiting.
-
`TestPoolProvideTxnsKeepsProvidingAfterTheStopOnceTheParentBlockIsSeen`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): with the stop channel already closed and the
parent already seen, 1000 calls must all return the decrypted
transaction. Without the tracker check, some calls returned no
transactions (20 of 20 runs failed).
- `TestBlockTrackerWaitReportsCancellationForAnUnseenBlock`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): a `synctest` context lets the waiter goroutine
finish before `Wait` selects, so both cases are ready. `Wait` must
return `context.Canceled` for a block it has not seen. Before: `nil`.
-
`TestProvideTxnsReportsCancellationWhenTheParentBlockWaitIsAlsoStopped`
(`txnprovider/txpool`): with the caller's context cancelled and the stop
closed, `ProvideTxns` must return `context.Canceled`. Before: `nil` for
some calls.
-
`TestPoolProvideTxnsFallsBackToBaseProviderWhenTheParentBlockWaitTimesOut`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): the parent never arrives and fake time passes
the one-slot deadline. `ProvideTxns` must return the base provider's
transactions and no error. Before: `issue while waiting for parent block
2: context deadline exceeded`.
- `TestBlockTrackerWaitReportsCancellationAfterTheTrackerStops`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): a stopped tracker and a cancelled context;
`Wait` must return `context.Canceled`. Before: `block tracker stopped`.
- `TestBlockTrackerWaitReturnsWhenCancelledRightAfterItsWaiterChecks`
(`txnprovider/shutter`): a test context is cancelled by the waiter's own
check, which still sees it as live, so the cancellation lands before the
waiter's `Cond.Wait`. `Wait` must return `context.Canceled`. Without the
lock around the broadcast: the wakeup was lost and `Wait` never returned
(5 of 5 runs).

Test harnesses: tests that call `getPayload` right after a forkchoice
update would otherwise depend on the txpool processing the new head
within the 500 ms grace. `ExecModuleTester.AssembleBlock` and
`MockCl.StartBuilding` (engine API tester) now wait, for at most a
minute, until the txpool has seen the parent block
(`txpoolwait.WaitForParent`), and the two Caplin block production tests
that build through the execution module directly call
`ExecModuleTester.WaitForTxPool`. For the engine API tester this needs a
`TxPool()` accessor on `eth.Ethereum`. With the grace set to 0 locally,
`TestAssembleBlockGasOverflow` and the whole `./execution/engineapi`
package still pass.

No new test for the txpool watcher change: it does not change behaviour,
and the existing tests in `pool_best_lock_test.go` cover the wait loop.

Refactor step: two helpers, `assembleWithTxPoolBehindParent` and
`newLoggingPool`, now hold the setup that the new tests share with
existing tests.

Mutation check: I removed each production piece on its own (passing the
option, waking the idle wait, closing the channel in `Stop`, the txpool
wait-loop case, the txpool wake-up case, the shutter cancellation, the
shutter "no transactions" return, and the state check in
`BlockTracker.Wait`). Each time, the test that covers it failed.

The new tests pass with `-count=20` and with `-race`. `go test` passes
for `./execution/builder/...`, `./execution/execmodule/...` and
`./txnprovider/...`. With `-race`, it passes for
`./execution/builder/...`, `./execution/execmodule`,
`./txnprovider/txpool/...` and `./txnprovider/shutter`.

author: lystopad
subject: cl/beacon/handler: retry payload preparation within the post-PTC window (#25207)
body:
Part of #24119 (item 2).

## Problem

After the wake-up at the PTC deadline, any skip (block work in flight,
an import, a still-pending payload path) waited for the next
quarter-slot tick. With 12 s slots that tick can come after the
state-work cutoff (10 s), so a short contention at the PTC deadline lost
the whole preparation window for a Gloas EMPTY path. #24939 and #24938
list this as a known limitation.

## Change

While the selected head is a current-slot Gloas head and no outcome has
settled for its target slot, the loop also wakes every `slot/48` (250 ms
on 12 s slots). It stops retrying when:
- an outcome settles (success, a memoized failure, `unchanged`, or a
FULL path that needs a fork-choice update), or
- the next retry would fall inside the state-work lead
(`stateWorkLead`), so no work starts after the existing cutoff.

Other slots keep the quarter-slot ticker. Normal production and the
gate, head and deadline checks are unchanged.

## Tests

`TestPreparePayloadLoopRetriesBusySkipAfterPTCDeadline` runs the real
loop and gate in `testing/synctest` with ticks at 3, 6, 9 and 12 s and
block work held from 8.999 s:
- block work ends at 9.1 s: exactly one attempt, after 9.1 s and before
the 10 s cutoff (on main: none);
- block work ends at 10.1 s: no attempt.

`go test -race ./cl/beacon/handler/` passes; `make lint` is clean twice;
`make erigon integration` builds.

author: Kewei
subject: cl/persistence: read Gloas queues before the first Gloas dump (#25212)
body:
Fixes #25200

## Problem

`ReadHistoricalState` reads `builders`, `builder_pending_withdrawals`
and `payload_expected_withdrawals` from the dump at `slot - slot %
SlotsPerDump` plus the per-slot diffs. `ReadRequiredQueueSSZ` returned
`ErrMissingGloasData` whenever that dump was missing. The antiquary
writes these dumps only for a Gloas state, so every state between the
Gloas fork slot and the first Gloas dump slot could not be read. On
Sepolia these are slots 11296768–11297279. The same happens for an
aligned fork slot whose block is missed.

## Fix

The change is reader-only. There is no antiquary change and no
persistence-format change.

- `ReadHistoricalState` passes the Gloas fork slot to
`ReadRequiredQueueSSZ`.
- A missing dump at or before the fork slot is read as an empty list.
The antiquary does not initialize the Gloas queue writers from a
pre-Gloas state, so the first Gloas diff holds the full list.
- In that case the replay starts at the dump slot itself, so a diff
stored there is not skipped. When the dump is present, the replay still
starts at the slot after it.
- A missing dump after the fork slot still returns
